#3232. Consumer Appetite for Personal AI Goes Mainstream

Nearly 70 percent of respondents say they want an AI assistant in their next device, according to a new report

Qualcomm builds intelligent, connected, computing and AI solutions that transform industries and advance human progress.

A recent report by Qualcomm Technologies, built on a survey of more than 12,000 people across key geographies worldwide, shows that around 70 percent of respondents express strong interest in an AI assistant that can interact naturally through voice and seamlessly manage devices, apps, and everyday tasks.

This article is brought to you by Qualcomm Technologies.

For many consumers, much of the promise and appeal of AI is personal. Consumers are looking past generic tools and want to know how these technologies will help them in their daily lives. These trends coincide with the advent of new classes of wearable devices that, in addition to being able to leverage powerful frontier models, feature built-in intelligence that understand the context of a user. Where are they? What are they seeing and hearing? What are their habits, their preferences, their schedules?

It’s an astonishing pivot, from passive accessories that served mostly to send users smartphone notifications to proactive, intelligent companions. The smartphone is no longer the center of that universe; though it’s still incredibly important, in this personal AI paradigm, the AI is the UI. And it shifts the focus toward you, the user.

These new technologies are exciting. But what do consumers really want?

A Personal AI report, commissioned by Qualcomm Technologies, built on a survey of more than 12,000 people across key geographies worldwide (the U.S., U.K., Germany, India, Brazil, and China) focused on the rise of personal AI in intelligent wearables looks deeply at these developments.

The smartphone is no longer the center of that universe; though it’s still incredibly important, in this personal AI paradigm, the AI is the UI.

Survey respondents are less interested in single devices and are responding more to the idea of connected ecosystems. As people expand their roster of devices, it only makes sense. Instead of relying entirely on a smartphone and a laptop, respondents also have connected technology in their cars, as well as intelligent wearables like smartwatches, smart glasses, hearables, and other wearables like rings, pins, and pendants. They want those devices to work in concert, and the way to do that is to decentralize any single one of them. Instead, the AI agent that knows the user and works across all of those devices becomes the unifying factor.

Consider a typical workday: A user’s watch detects it is time to leave for a meeting and, with permission, their AI agent factors in calendar details, real-time traffic and battery status across their devices. In the car, it suggests the best route and briefs them on their meeting agenda. As they arrive, smart glasses surface a discreet reminder, such as the meeting location or the name of a new contact, while the phone stays in their pocket. No one device has to do everything; each plays the role it is best suited for, coordinated by a personal AI agent that understands the user’s context and acts only at the user’s direction.

With this in mind, simply adding more hardware to the mix isn’t sufficient. Even though respondents will be open to new form factors, they’ll demand more from their ecosystem of devices. They’ll be sensitive to points of friction and needless complexity, and they’ll require each new device to bring something new to the table — “incremental intelligence, convenience, or contextual awareness that their existing devices cannot deliver on their own what the report,” reads the report.

The usage trends are up. The report found that those who own wearables are already using AI frequently (60 percent use it at least weekly), which indicates that it’s becoming less of a fun experiment for early adopters and more of a critical mass habit.

The “always-on” nature of intelligent wearables appears to be winning respondents, too. The report found the following statistics on average continuous wear among users:

But for all the excitement and engagement around intelligent wearables, there’s a gating factor: trust. As use cases for intelligent wearables expands to more personal and persistent experiences, trust is a necessity for Personal AI.

Notably, the report found that respondents expressed more interest in adopting intelligent wearables when Snapdragon was introduced as the enabling platform. This reinforces the value of having an established, trusted technology foundation in the mix.

The report shows that consumer appetite for AI is high, with 60-70 percent of those surveyed expressing interest in advanced AI as they consider a new device. That’s a constant. But remaining purchase drivers differed between device categories.

Audio playback quality is the most influential purchase driver for true wireless earbuds and headphones. For smartwatches, it’s display quality and responsiveness. Respondents are less concerned about technical specifications than aesthetics like materials and finish when it comes to devices like smart rings and pendants. And for smart glasses, it’s all about the type of control, whether it’s voice, gesture, or touch.

Artificial intelligence is entering a new phase, one that is deeply personal, continuously present, and seamlessly embedded into the devices we wear every day. This evolution, which we define as “Personal AI”, represents a shift away from generic, cloud-only intelligence toward AI that understands individuals in context: their habits, preferences, environments, and intent, in real time.

Alongside these purchase drivers is another key finding: Consumer appetite for Personal AI agents has gone mainstream. The report says that 70 percent of respondents “express strong interest in an AI assistant that can interact naturally through voice and seamlessly manage devices, apps, and everyday tasks.” With each individual as the center of their own ecosystem, voice becomes the most critical, natural method for interacting with agents.

Intelligent wearables comprise much of the hardware of this “ecosystem of you.” Consumers are interested in ecosystems instead of single devices, and they’re looking for agentic AI capabilities that understand and act on their behalf.

Yet so much of the industry remains undefined. OEMs and technology makers have an enormous opportunity right now to innovate and iterate on the strong technological foundations that platform makers are building. And the roadmap for what consumers want is clear.

All percentages, consumer behaviors, and attitudes stated in this report are based only on the responses of the individuals who participated in our survey.

Qualcomm Technologies is a global leader in communications and computing technologies, including leading-edge AI, high-performance, low-power computing, and connectivity solutions. Headquartered in San Diego, Calif., the company develops technologies for next-generation mobile networks and smart devices, and designs semiconductors such as mobile processors and AI chips.

The bias is deafening. Qualcomm, a chip manufacturer that is all in on AI, makes a survey and then states they found everyone loves using AI, the very AI that will run on Qualcomm chips. Clearly they don't have a conflict of interest in this. /s

#3228. Multiphysics Modeling for Next-Generation Electromagnetic Manufacturing Technologies



Advances in sensing, manufacturing, computational resources, and data-driven methods are enabling new approaches to electromagnetic sensing, non-destructive evaluation, and advanced materials processing. This webinar will demonstrate how the COMSOL Multiphysics software supports predictive modeling by coupling electromagnetic fields with thermal, chemical, mechanical, and transport phenomena across multiple length and time scales.

The first application we will show focuses on eddy-current thermometry for reconstructing three-dimensional temperature fields in metal plates. Temperature-dependent electrical conductivity alters induced currents and magnetic fields, enabling volumetric thermal inference. COMSOL simulations of defects and laser-induced transient heating will support validation of reconstruction algorithms. Multifrequency excitation will be investigated to improve depth discrimination through frequency-dependent penetration depths and sensitivities.

The second application examines microwave-enabled volumetric additive manufacturing of ceramic components. A high-power microwave beamforming array delivers localized energy into three-dimensional volumes, enabling processing of opaque, particle-laden resins. Coupled COMSOL models of electromagnetic propagation, microwave absorption, heat transfer, and ceramic sintering kinetics are used to predict temperature evolution, reaction progression, spatial resolution, and processing scalability. Future extensions will incorporate pulsed excitation, fluid flow, resin viscosity, convection, shrinkage, and solid mechanics.

Together, these examples demonstrate how the COMSOL software can integrate multiphysics modeling with sensing, manufacturing, and data inversion. This webinar will present two applications of coupled electromagnetic and thermal modeling in COMSOL Multiphysics: eddy-current thermometry in metal plates and microwave-assisted processing of ceramic-loaded resins. By connecting simulation with practical engineering systems, COMSOL-based modeling can accelerate technology development, reduce experimental iteration, and support reliable scale-up of next-generation electromagnetic technologies.

#3227. Apple offers a military discount, here’s how to get it

If you’re a member of the U.S. military, Apple offers an easy way to save 10% on eligible products and accessories. It’s available to current and veteran members of the U.S. military and their immediate family members living in the same household. While you’ll need to verify your eligibility to access the discount, the process is simple. There are also a few limitations you’ll want to know about before placing an order. Here’s everything you need to know.

A 10% discount is available to current and Veteran members of the US Military, National Guard and Reserve. Immediate family members who reside in the same household are also eligible.

Verification is handled through ID.me. Creating an ID.me account is free, and current military members can verify their service using their .mil email address. Veterans can enter details of their service information for ID.me to verify, or upload images of official documents (such as a DD-214) for ID.me to review and confirm their eligibility. Once you’re verified, your ID.me account can also be used to access military discounts from other retailers and services that support ID.me verification.

Once verified, you can start shopping by visiting Apple’s Store for Veterans and Military. The discount only applies to Apple products and accessories (including Beats) so third-party products aren’t eligible. Apple services, such as Apple Music and iCloud+, are also excluded. Orders can be shipped directly to you, or you can choose in-store pickup if the product is available at a nearby Apple Store.

This is probably the biggest catch. Apple specifically says ACMI isn’t available when shopping through the Veterans and Military Store. You can still earn 3% back in Daily Cash with Apple Card, but you lose the option to finance your purchase at 0% interest over several months. Apple Upgrade also isn’t available when purchasing through the military store.

The only way to get the military discount is to make your purchase through Apple’s website in a browser. The Apple Store app isn’t an option, which means you also can’t take advantage of Apple’s “Get Ready” feature to select your iPhone model, color, storage capacity, and carrier ahead of pre-orders opening. Instead, you’ll have to navigate Apple’s website on launch day, when demand is high and server traffic can make checkout more challenging. Whether the 10% savings is worth giving up the convenience of a potentially quicker checkout is ultimately up to you.

The military discount can’t be combined with carrier promotions or discounts on iPhone purchases. You can still trade in your existing iPhone through Apple and receive the applicable trade-in value, but you can’t take advantage of carrier-specific trade-in offers, like promotions that give you a larger credit when you trade in an eligible device and activate or upgrade a line.

These purchase limits reset on January 1 each year.

Apple’s military discount is a useful perk, especially if you’re buying a product at launch and want to save 10% right away. However, it’s worth comparing prices with other retailers before you buy, since sales and promotions can sometimes beat Apple’s discount. The military store also comes with a few limitations, so you’ll want to weigh the savings against the features and payment options you’re giving up. Even with those caveats, 10% off can make a real difference on an expensive Apple purchase.

#3226. Prince Harry urges EU to make tech firms prove apps are safe for children

At the Lost Screen Memorial in Brussels, Harry backed the EU Kids Act and called for an end to the infinite scroll. He also named Meta, Google and TikTok for fighting California’s limits.

Prince Harry speaks at the opening of the Lost Screen Memorial at the European Parliament in Brussels on 10 November 2026.

Prince Harry wants tech companies, not parents, to carry the burden of child safety online. He told the European Parliament on Tuesday that firms must show that children can use their products safely. He spoke in Brussels at the opening of the Lost Screen Memorial. It honours children whose parents link their deaths to harm on social media.

The memorial shows replicas of oversized smartphones, each with a child’s photo on the home screen, the Associated Press reported. It opened in New York last year with support from the couple’s Archewell charity, according to the BBC. Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, attended but withdrew from speaking, the AP reported.

“Parents should not have to prove that a product is dangerous. Companies should have to demonstrate that it is safe for children. The details can be phased in, but that principle cannot wait,” Harry said.

Harry urged MEPs to go further with the EU Kids Act. The Commission proposed it in September, with a ban on social media for under-13s. He said the law should tackle addictive design and treat a seven-year-old and a 15-year-old differently. Age limits alone, he added, “cannot be the answer”.

He singled out the infinite scroll. Young people told him that endless short videos marked the moment things got worse. He said banning the feature should be simple. He then named the companies fighting such limits. Meta, Google and TikTok had challenged California’s rules on addictive features, he said.

The three companies sued California last week over AB 1709, Colin Lecher reported for CalMatters. The law bars features such as infinite scroll, autoplay and recommendations for under-16s from January. The companies argue that it breaks their free speech rights. In its complaint, Meta said the law would make the state “the editor, curator, and controller of online speech”.

“Overly broad laws like this actually break the systems we’ve built to help kids find high-quality, age-appropriate videos,” Google spokesperson José Castañeda told CalMatters.

He told the panel that a “handful of very powerful people” want a “lawless” social media world, Politico reported. He praised the Kids Act for putting the burden of proof on companies. Members of the internal market committee, which leads the Parliament’s talks on the law, were in the room.

Harry made a similar case about AI in New York in September. He warned then that AI companion chatbots want children’s attachment. In Brussels, he said AI is now “taking over our relationships”.

The Commission is already acting on parts of his list. It has accused TikTok of building a ‘rabbit hole’ feed under the Digital Services Act. It has also asked member states to pause national bans on social media for a year.

Prime Video's Lord of the Rings series returns with a new season. Here is a quick refresher.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Mr. Tolkien, we meet again. After a two-year hiatus, “The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power” returns to Prime Video for its third season. The war is in full swing, as Sauron and his nefarious forces move quickly to take over Middle-earth. However, the Elves, the Dwarves, and the people of Númenor plan to defend their world to the bitter end.

To (mis)quote Boromir at the Council of Elrond, “One does not simply return to Mordor without a refresher course.” While I’m pleased that “The Rings of Power” is back, it’s difficult to remember every storyline and plot point when new seasons have been released every other year since 2022. Here are five things to remember before embarking on another journey set in Middle-earth.

Sauron is not a good guy. Not a good guy at all! In season 1, Sauron (Charlie Vickers) appeared as Halbrand, a drifter fleeing from the Orcs who befriends Galadriel (Morfydd Clark). By the end of the season, Halbrand reveals himself as Sauron and asks Galadriel to rule alongside him, which she vehemently rejects.

In season 2, Sauron convinces Celebrimbor (Charles Edwards) that he is an elf named Annatar. Sauron manipulates Celebrimbor into forging the Rings of Power. After killing Celebrimbor, Sauron attacks Galadriel and steals the Nine Rings of Power for Men. While surveying his kingdom in Mordor, Sauron becomes fixated on one mission: forging the One Ring to rule Middle-earth. The making of the One Ring is arguably the most anticipated moment in the show to this point.

Welcome to the party, Gandalf! For the majority of the two seasons, Daniel Weyman played “The Stranger,” a mysterious bearded wizard who fell from the sky. The Stranger befriended Nori (Markella Kavenagh) from the Harfoots’ clan. After saving Nori and Poppy (Megan Richards) from the Dark Wizard, the Stranger and Nori decide to go their separate ways.

Enter Tom Bombadil (Rory Kinnear), the legendary character from Tolkien’s “The Lord of the Rings.” The Stranger returns to Tom Bombadil and takes a branch to use as a magic staff. It’s here that we learn that the Stranger is Gandalf—yes, the illustrious wizard played by Ian McKellen in Peter Jackson’s trilogy. Selfishly, it'll be much easier to call this character Gandalf rather than the Stranger, the Giant, or the Big Fella.

“The Rings of Power” season 3 will not pick up in the immediate aftermath of the season 2 finale. Instead, the series will feature a time jump five years into the future. Co‑showrunner Patrick McKay told SFX Magazine that the time jump brings the action to the “tipping point” of the war between Sauron’s armies and the Elves.

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

Think of the time jump as a soft reboot. Many of the same characters return for season 3, but it’s a fresh start for the story as a whole. The showrunners have a lot of ground to cover in Middle-earth’s Second Age, one of which I’ll discuss later. The showrunners originally envisioned the series as a five-season saga, so expect more time jumps to occur in the future.

So far, we talked about the Elves and Gandalf. One of the primary races in “The Rings of Power” is the dwarves, who live in the underground realm of Khazad-dûm in the Misty Mountains. In season 2, King Durin III (Peter Mullan) became corrupted by his Ring of Power and dug deeper into the mountain to mine mithril. It was a catastrophic mistake, as Durin III awoke the Balrog, a fiery, demonic creature. Left with no other choice, Durin III attacked the Balrog, sacrificing himself by causing the cavern to collapse and burying himself alongside the creature.

When season 3 begins, Durin IV (Owain Arthur) is the newly crowned king and, more importantly, has the ring that drove his father mad. However, Durin III’s sacrifice did not destroy the Balrog. In season 3, Sauron will confront the Balrog as he seeks to uncover the secrets of forging the One Ring. That’s not all. The Balrog will speak for the first time on-screen, with Simon Pegg providing the voice. Unfortunately, I’m not expecting Pegg to provide comedic relief as he did as Benji in the “Mission: Impossible” franchise.

I debated whether to include this point about Númenor as one of the five things to remember before the season. Is it a spoiler if you already know Númenor’s fate? I won’t reveal it explicitly, but most viewers can tell that Númenor is in trouble. After Queen Regent Míriel (Cynthia Addai-Robinson) went blind, cracks began to appear in Númenor's metaphorical armor. Then, Pharazôn (Trystan Gravelle) successfully seized the throne in a coup, as his King’s Men faction arrested the remaining members of the Faithful.

Under Pharazôn and the King’s Men, Númenor is in a horrible place due to the political instability and a hatred of the Elves. The kingdom is heading in the wrong direction. There are still several major storylines to play out in Númenor, but let's just say that if things don't change, the kingdom is heading toward its end.

“The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power” season 3 has an interesting release schedule on Prime Video. The first four episodes premiere on November 11. Episodes 5-6 will stream on November 18, and the final two episodes of the season will air on November 25. So mark those dates in your calendar now!

#3224. When Electric Cars Were for Women

Early carmakers decided women wanted cars that were quiet, clean, and easy to start

Allison Marsh is a professor at the University of South Carolina and the codirector of the Ann Johnson Institute for Science, Technology & Society.

When automobiles were still a novelty, electric cars vied with those powered by steam and internal combustion.

At the turn of the last century, the automobile industry was still new and evolving rapidly. In 1898, there were about 50 carmakers in the United States. A decade later, that number had increased fivefold. In 1901, the companies produced 7,000 vehicles. By 1910, production had reached 181,000.

For several decades, electric cars vied with those powered by steam and internal combustion, and nobody was sure which technology would come out on top. Steam had the legacy of locomotive technology behind it but came with a risk of fire. Steam-powered vehicles could also become exceedingly hot, depending on the placement of the boiler and the steam piping. Both gasoline and electric cars faced logistical challenges: How far could you travel without refueling or charging? You could always throw an extra can of gasoline in the back of the car, but charging a battery involved more planning. The infrastructure for long-distance travel was not yet in place.

Before the invention of the electric starter in 1911, gasoline-powered engines had to be started with a hand crank; once running, they were loud and emitted noxious fumes. Fully electric vehicles, by contrast, were easy to start; you just turned on the main battery switch, often with a key, and there was no foul exhaust to deal with.

Electric carmakers looking for a way to differentiate their products decided that these attributes made their vehicles perfect for women. (Electric cars were also marketed to doctors so that they could make house calls in the middle of the night without waking the neighbors.) General Electric, which made car chargers based on mercury-arc rectifiers, was so captivated by the idea of women driving electric cars that the company created a series of advertisements featuring stylishly dressed women plugging in their cars and posing with their charging stations.

In ads for its electric car chargers, General Electric featured women using the equipment.miSci—Museum of Innovation and Science

A young woman named Fannie Goodnow was an early EV adopter. She owned a 1908 Bailey Victoria Phaeton, an open two-seater that really did look like a horseless carriage, and she used a GE mercury-arc rectifier to charge it.

Electrical engineer Peter Cooper Hewitt invented the mercury vapor lamp, which became the basis for the mercury-arc rectifier used in car-charging systems. Bettmann/Getty Images

Electrical engineer Peter Cooper Hewitt is generally credited with the invention of the mercury-arc rectifier. During the first decade of the 20th century, Hewitt received several U.S. patents for electric lamps and other apparatus for transmitting and using electric currents. U.S. patents 968,896 and 1,163,706, granted to Percy H. Thomas, advanced Hewitt’s designs. Thomas was chief electrician for the Cooper Hewitt Electric Co., which Hewitt had cofounded with George Westinghouse to manufacture and sell his lamps.

The mercury-arc rectifier functioned as a diode. In a car charger like the one Fannie Goodnow used, it converted alternating current from the power grid into direct current needed to charge the car’s battery. A small amount of liquid mercury contained in a glass tube would vaporize and glow as electricity passed through it. Coupled with the carbon anodes, the vapor allowed current to flow in only one direction. This unit took about 12 hours to charge a drained battery.

I couldn’t find any records as to why Fannie Goodnow opted for an electric car. But as a well-to-do woman living in the Boston area, she had more than a half dozen automobile producers to choose from. The one she chose was S.R. Bailey & Co. of Amesbury, Mass.

This early electric car charger used a mercury-arc rectifier to convert AC to DC.Heritage Museums & Gardens

According to Galen Handy, who maintains the Early Electric Vehicles website, Samuel Robinson Bailey started in the carriage and sleigh business as a teenager, winning a best-in-show prize at a carriage exhibition in Portland, Maine, in 1855. Bailey developed a reputation as an inventor and designed processes to streamline the manufacture of his vehicles. He went into business for himself in 1882. Just over a decade later, one of Bailey’s carriages won a gold medal at the 1893 World’s Columbian Exposition in Chicago.

Bailey’s son Edwin attended the exposition, where he likely would have seen a vision of the future: the Morrison electric wagon. This six-passenger, battery-powered vehicle ferried visitors and VIPs around the fairgrounds. It wasn’t long before automobiles began eating into the carriage business. In December 1906, with the carriage industry collapsing, S.R. Bailey & Co. announced it was getting into electric vehicles.

Bailey’s first model, the Victoria Phaeton, used an Edison alkaline battery. Thomas Edison had been working on a lighter, more reliable, and more powerful battery for the auto industry since the 1890s, and announced the achievement with great fanfare in 1903. Unfortunately for Bailey and other carmakers who deployed it, the battery leaked and wouldn’t hold a charge. Edison was forced to go back to the drawing board. By 1910, he had a better battery in production, but by then his friend Henry Ford had introduced the Model T, setting the stage for the internal combustion engine to take over the market.

While Edison toiled to improve his tech, Bailey pivoted to a battery from the Gould Storage Battery Co. of Depew, N.Y. Gould also supplied batteries for railroads, utilities, subways, elevators, and farms. Goodnow’s Victoria Phaeton used a 30-cell lead-acid battery housed in a wooden box that was suspended under the chassis. The standard battery had a range of 64 to 80 kilometers; a larger battery with 50 percent more capacity was available for an upcharge. With the standard battery, the Victoria Phaeton cost US $2,000 (about $73,000 today, or about the list price of an upscale EV like the Audi Q8 or BMW i5).

Fannie Goodnow’s electric car charger now resides at the Heritage Museums & Gardens in Sandwich, Mass. But her 1908 Bailey Victoria Phaeton has been lost to history. Shown here is a 1911 version of that model.Sarah Thornington/Heritage Museums & Gardens

Goodnow installed a mercury-arc rectifier charging station in the barn adjacent to her parents’ summer home in Hull, Mass. Bill Lillie of Vintage Electric Cars notes that the charging plug was of an unusual design. This is, of course, one of the banes of any early adopter: nonstandardized plugs and cables. The Electric Vehicle Association of America, which formed in 1910, tried to put forward a standard so that electric vehicles could be charged at any charging station. (Modern EV owners can no doubt relate.) But savvy electric car owners knew to carry spare plug adapters and cables when traveling.

When Edison’s improved battery was finally available, Bailey began using it in the Victoria Phaeton and then went on a publicity blitz. In September 1910, the carmaker sponsored a round-trip tour from New York to Boston, with a side trip up New Hampshire’s Mount Washington, totaling about 1,600 km. Sadly, the “This Car Climbed Mt. Washington” bumper sticker hadn’t yet become popular.

Thomas Edison supplied the batteries for an electric car made by S.R. Bailey & Co., which then went on a publicity road trip from New York to Boston. miSci—Museum of Innovation and Science

Although Thomas Edison posed for a photo with the new Bailey Victoria Phaeton that featured his new battery, he himself chose a Detroit Electric Victoria for his own use. (Edison was known to be a terrible driver, so someone else likely chauffeured him around.)

Unable to compete against the rising tide of Model Ts, S.R. Bailey sold its factory in 1915, having produced about 500 to 600 electric vehicles.

Although the vehicle Fannie Goodnow chose turned out to be just a blip in automotive history, I like to imagine her driving about town in a beautiful car that embodied all the quirks of early adoption. I hope her friends didn’t make fun of her for investing in electric just before internal combustion took off. I hope she didn’t get stranded without the proper charging cable. I do not know what happened to her or her Victoria Phaeton, but her charging station remained in situ until 2022, when it was donated to the Heritage Museums & Gardens in Sandwich, Mass. Now it stands ready to tell stories of technological change and adoption that continue to resonate today.

Part of a continuing series looking at historical artifacts that embrace the boundless potential of technology.

An abridged version of this article appears in the November 2026 print issue.

References For a detailed history of the development of the mercury-arc rectifier (or valve), see Deepak Tiku’s article in the March/April 2014 issue of IEEE Power & Energy Magazine.Harry Cooke Cushing Jr., a fellow of the American Institute of Electrical Engineers, wrote (and updated regularly over a number of years) The Electric Vehicle Hand-Book, which gave general instructions for the care and storage of batteries, including how to charge them with a mercury-arc rectifier. Discussion of the mercury-arc rectifier begins on page 156 of the 10th edition, published in 1922. (The American Institute of Electrical Engineers is one of the predecessor organizations of the IEEE.)

For a detailed history of the development of the mercury-arc rectifier (or valve), see Deepak Tiku’s article in the March/April 2014 issue of IEEE Power & Energy Magazine.

Harry Cooke Cushing Jr., a fellow of the American Institute of Electrical Engineers, wrote (and updated regularly over a number of years) The Electric Vehicle Hand-Book, which gave general instructions for the care and storage of batteries, including how to charge them with a mercury-arc rectifier. Discussion of the mercury-arc rectifier begins on page 156 of the 10th edition, published in 1922. (The American Institute of Electrical Engineers is one of the predecessor organizations of the IEEE.)

Allison Marsh is a professor in Women and Gender Studies at the University of South Carolina and codirector of the university’s Ann Johnson Institute for Science, Technology & Society. She combines her interests in engineering, history, and museum objects to write the Past Forward column, which tells the story of technology through historical artifacts. Marsh is currently working on a book on the history of women in electrical engineering.

#3222. Guarding the Gates of Knowledge

AI can fake a plausible paper at the push of a button. Can detection tools and peer review keep up?

Harry Goldstein is Editor in Chief of IEEE Spectrum.

A recent scroll through social media got me thinking about trust. About half my feed was filled with AI slop that astute users would call out as being machine-generated, often to the embarrassment of the rube who unknowingly spread it and sometimes to the delight of the poster who shared it deliberately because they found it amusing or useful for sowing confusion.

Remember the good old days of GPT-3 when we could ask the chatbot anything and it would almost instantly and very confidently spit back a plausible but false answer? That’s when the word “hallucination” as applied to AI answers entered the lexicon. Six years and several versions of a few different chatbots later, I still can’t trust the answers I get, even though Claude or Gemini often do useful work for me. That’s the thing about current AI: Trust but verify. And verify you must.

Apply that maxim at scale to maintain the integrity of the scientific record and you get an idea of the challenge facing publishers of peer-reviewed scholarship. In “I Used AI to Fake a Scientific Paper,” freelance writer and doctor of applied mathematics Benjamin Skuse tells the story of the human gatekeepers trying to beat back the rising tide of AI slop by attempting to get his own AI-generated papers past IEEE’s defenses.

“He basically hit ‘run experiment’ and ‘write paper.’ And then he didn’t do a damn thing to it.” —Eliza Strickland

As features and AI beat editor Eliza Strickland told me, Skuse was surprised at just how effortless it was to generate a paper that was more or less plausible and more or less science. For one of his experiments, “he basically hit ‘run experiment’ and ‘write paper,’” she said. “And then he didn’t do a damn thing to it. He just launched it into the maw of the publishing engine.”

Skuse discovered that the combination of IEEE’s human-review processes and research-integrity checker programs are currently keeping pace in what amounts to a cat-and-mouse game against people using free tools. But the more advanced LLMs are no longer making the same dumb mistakes the free versions do. That leaves publishers locked in an arms race between increasingly plausible slop and the systems aimed at detecting it.

Scholarly publishers aren’t the only ones trying to hold the line against slop. So is that global depository of human-generated knowledge, Wikipedia. For this month’s Five Questions, Strickland interviewed Ellia Lebleu, a founding member of WikiProject AI Cleanup, a volunteer effort to detect and delete AI-generated material from the platform. Lebleu’s team is confronting the same problem as commercial publishers, but with fewer people and fewer tools.

“Wikipedia is known as a repository of human-generated information, and they want to hold on to that,” says Strickland. “Who knows how long they’ll be able to do that.”

If we can’t collectively assume that the scientific record is trustworthy or that basic facts about the world are accurate, then our understanding of what is real unspools into uncertainty. Perhaps that delights quantum scientists and the grifters who thrive in an information environment where there is no shared reality. But that uncertainty ultimately undermines trust in the institutions that exist to curate the corpus of human knowledge and to promote the advancement of science and technology for the benefit of humanity.

Or maybe in a world where AI is doing the science and writing the papers, it won’t matter whether or not humans trust the outputs. As Strickland put it, “Doesn’t it just feel crazy that we’ll have AI writing for other AIs at some point? We’ll just get left out of the loop.”

Harry Goldstein is Editor in Chief of IEEE Spectrum.

#3220. Terra Security brings continuous, agentic offensive security to every layer

Terra Security combines agentic pentesting with offensive security researchers to test AI systems, networks and web applications continuously. The company says testing that took weeks can take hours.

Cybersecurity teams have spent years trying to close the gap between discovering vulnerabilities and addressing them. Traditional penetration testing remains an important part of security programs. But its periodic nature creates an inherent limitation. The results represent a snapshot of an environment that may already have changed by the time testing is complete.

That challenge is becoming more difficult as organizations accelerate software development, expand their cloud infrastructure and introduce artificial intelligence into business operations. New applications, integrations and AI systems create additional potential entry points. Development cycles increasingly outpace the traditional security assessments designed to evaluate them.

The problem is not simply the growing number of vulnerabilities. It is the speed at which new attack paths emerge. It is also the difficulty of determining which ones pose meaningful risks to a particular business.

Terra Security is building its platform around this changing reality. Its approach combines agentic artificial intelligence with skilled offensive security researchers to test, validate, and remediate AI systems, network infrastructure, and web applications. Rather than treating pentesting as a scheduled exercise, the company is positioning it as an ongoing security capability that adapts alongside the organization.

Traditional penetration testing typically operates within defined engagements. Security teams scope an assessment, coordinate testing, review findings, and then prioritize remediation. Depending on the complexity of the environment, that process can take weeks, leaving opportunities for vulnerabilities to emerge between assessments.

Terra Platform™ is designed to shorten that cycle considerably. The company says its agentic pentesting technology can reduce testing timelines from four to six weeks to approximately a matter of hours. That represents an improvement of up to 250 times compared with traditional approaches.

The distinction extends beyond speed. Terra designed its agents to operate continuously, analyzing environments as they evolve rather than waiting for the next scheduled assessment. This gives security teams a way to identify vulnerabilities as they emerge and evaluate their implications while the surrounding systems and business context are still current.

That capability is particularly relevant as AI development introduces new categories of potential exposure. Organizations are deploying AI applications, connecting models to internal systems and giving agents access to data and business processes. These developments expand the attack surface in ways that conventional application and infrastructure testing may not fully address.

Terra brings these areas together through a single platform. It allows organizations to assess AI systems alongside their network infrastructure and web applications rather than managing separate offensive security processes for each.

One of the persistent challenges in vulnerability management is distinguishing technical findings from genuine business risks. Automated security tools can generate substantial volumes of alerts, but not every vulnerability carries the same consequences. Without an understanding of how an application operates, what data it handles, and how it connects to other systems, security teams can spend considerable time investigating issues with limited practical impact.

Terra’s approach incorporates business context and code into the way its agents conduct assessments. The objective is to make testing more relevant to the organization’s actual environment. It helps surface vulnerabilities and attack paths that could have meaningful consequences rather than simply producing longer lists of findings.

This distinction matters as organizations increasingly rely on automated security testing. More frequent assessments can improve coverage. But they can also create additional work if the resulting findings are not sufficiently prioritized. By grounding its agents in the organization’s business logic and technical environment, Terra aims to make continuous testing more actionable.

The company also argues that unifying offensive security capabilities can improve operational efficiency. According to Terra, organizations can achieve four times the return on investment through reduced workload, without increasing headcount or security budgets.

The growing use of AI agents in cybersecurity introduces another consideration. That is how much autonomy organizations should give automated systems, particularly when testing production environments.

Terra addresses this through what it calls a Human-on-the-Loop model. Rather than positioning its agents as independent operators with unrestricted authority, the platform incorporates human oversight at critical decision points to help maintain production safety and compliance.

The company’s Terra Offensive Research Collaboration Hub (TORCH) provides a workspace where security professionals can interact directly with agents, guide investigations, and control different stages of the testing process. This creates a collaborative model in which AI handles the scale and speed of continuous assessment. Security practitioners retain oversight of consequential decisions.

The approach reflects a broader question emerging across enterprise AI adoption. How can organizations benefit from autonomous systems without surrendering control over activities that require accountability?

As enterprise environments become more dynamic, security programs built around periodic assessments may struggle to keep pace with the systems they are intended to protect. The challenge is no longer limited to finding vulnerabilities during a scheduled engagement. It is maintaining meaningful visibility into an attack surface that changes continuously.

Terra Security is betting that offensive security will increasingly move toward this continuous model. By bringing AI systems, networks and web applications into one platform, while keeping human researchers involved in critical decisions, the company is seeking to make penetration testing a persistent part of security operations.

In a market where automation is becoming increasingly common, the differentiator may ultimately be how effectively technology combines speed, context and human judgment. For Terra, the objective is to make that combination available across every attack vector that matters.

With limited supplies, rising tides and no immediate help, she faces a desperate fight to survive.

Why you should watch it: "The Shallows" is a great choice when you're after a tense survival thriller that gets straight to the action. Blake Lively carries the film with a convincing physical performance, while director Jaume Collet-Serra makes the most of its isolated setting and terrifying underwater encounters. There's very little padding here, with the 87-minute runtime keeping the story focused and the tension consistently high. It's a particularly good watch if you enjoy shark movies.

#3218. IEEE Computer Society Chapter Offers Webinars With Industry Experts

Attendees in Region 4 learn about AI, cybersecurity, and more

Siva Rama Krishna Varma Bayyavarapu is an IEEE senior member and secretary of the IEEE Computer Society’s Central Indiana Chapter.

To help engineers keep up with emerging technologies such as AI, cloud computing, and sustainable infrastructure, and learn how they can be applied in practice, the IEEE Computer Society’s Central Indiana Chapter recently launched its Tech Talk Series.

The live webinar series connects IEEE members, undergrad and graduate students, and engineering professionals from IEEE Region 4 with industry practitioners. The monthly sessions have covered AI governance and security, agentic systems, and related topics. The sessions featured speakers from Apple, software company Tavant, and cybersecurity concern Zscaler.

Upcoming sessions and registration details are available on the IEEE Region 4 virtual events calendar.

Rather than presenting on emerging technologies only at a conceptual level, speakers discussed the design decisions behind specific tools and systems, how the systems are structured, and implementation challenges. They also shared lessons learned from using the tools in their daily work.

Sessions also include technical walkthroughs and practical examples.

The live format allows attendees to discuss and compare their approaches when evaluating and implementing new technologies with those used by other organizations.

The organizers chose to make the series virtual so that chapter members and other attendees could participate in technical discussions with engineers from major technology companies and eliminate the need to travel.

For young professionals, the sessions connect what they’ve learned in a classroom with the realities of the workplace.

Technical programs such as the Tech Talk Series give professionals and students access to expertise, help create connections across career levels, and make important engineering discussions available to a broader community.

Attendees learn how practitioners approach projects such as system architecture, reliability, security, governance, and product delivery. For experienced professionals, the talks offer a forum to examine new ways of designing, securing, and operating software systems, and compare technical approaches. They can ask questions relevant to systems being evaluated or deployed within their organization.

The most recent webinar, Feeding and Fencing AI Agents: Engineering Governed Agentic Systems on Real-Time Data, featured Gajendra Babu Thokala, a senior engineering leader at Apple in Seattle.

The IEEE senior member explained how teams can move beyond adding isolated AI features to applications and instead build governed AI-agent systems that use real-time business data to complete multistep business workflows.

Another recent session, Building AI Native Products: A Playbook for Agentic Systems, explored how products built around AI agents differ from traditional software. It also covered how agentic systems can help users complete multistep tasks and workflows. IEEE Senior Member Sandeep Shivam, a product and technology leader at Tavant in Dallas, led the webinar.

Those two sessions illustrate the series’ purpose: helping participants understand what a technology can do and what is required to use it responsibly.

Future sessions are being planned on areas including enterprise AI, software reliability, and responsible AI usage. In addition to speakers from technology companies, the chapter also plans to invite speakers from startups, universities, and research organizations.

Upcoming sessions are expected to cover cloud platforms, enterprise integrations, and the responsible development of AI systems.

Technical programs such as the Tech Talk Series give professionals and students access to expertise, help create connections across career levels, and make important engineering discussions available to a broader community.

Undergraduate and graduate students are invited to participate to gain exposure to technical decision-making and challenges encountered in professional engineering environments.

Siva Rama Krishna Varma Bayyavarapu is an IEEE senior member and the secretary of the IEEE Computer Society Central Indiana Chapter. He is also the chair of the IEEE Central Indiana Student Activities Committee.

#3217. Top Wall Street analysts like these 3 dividend stocks for solid returns

The Federal Reserve indicated the possibility of a rate hike this year after its latest meeting, which could have implications for income-seeking investors.

Given this backdrop, dividend-paying stocks with strong yields and upside potential could help investors earn attractive returns.

Backed by solid research, top Wall Street analysts can provide key insights to pick stocks having the ability to generate compelling capital appreciation and pay consistent dividends, driven by solid fundamentals.

Here are three dividend-paying stocks that are highlighted by Wall Street's top pros, as tracked by TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Kinetik is a midstream company operating in the Delaware basin. With a quarterly dividend of 81 cents per share (annualized dividend of $3.24 per share), KNTK stock offers a dividend yield of about 7%.

RBC Capital analyst Elvira Scotto reiterated a buy rating on Kinetik stock and increased her price target to $53 from $50, citing expected growth from the KL2 project and sour gas opportunity in New Mexico. Scotto updated her estimates to reflect Kinetik's Q1 2026 results, with adjusted EBITDA beating estimates, driven by improved margins and Gulf Coast marketing gains that offset Waha price-related shut-ins.

The five-star analyst expects the Waha price-related shut-ins to persist until incremental takeaway capacity comes online later this year. Scotto said that Kinetik is well-positioned to capture New Mexico sour gas growth prospects when prices support activity. She sees the Northern Delaware Basin in New Mexico as a major growth opportunity for Kinetik. Scotto highlighted that Kinetik has purpose-built its system for sour gas handling, giving it an edge over new competitors that may face permitting delays of at least three years to build acid gas injection wells.

Additionally, Scotto pointed out Kinetik's attractive capital return framework, which targets a 3.5x to 4.0x leverage ratio, 3% to 5% hike in annual dividend until dividend coverage reaches 1.6x, and opportunistic share buybacks.

"We still view KNTK as a logical takeout candidate for buyers seeking to increase equity NGL barrels and sour gas processing," said Scotto.

Scotto ranks No. 211 among more than 12,300 analysts tracked by TipRanks. Her ratings have been successful 68% of the time, delivering an average return of 16%. See Kinetik Financials on TipRanks.

Oilfield services company SLB (SLB), formerly known as Schlumberger, is this week's second dividend pick. The company announced a quarterly cash dividend of nearly 30 cents per share, payable on July 9. At an annualized dividend of $1.18 per share, SLB stock offers a dividend yield of 2.5%.

Recently, Goldman Sachs analyst Neil Mehta reiterated a buy rating on SLB stock with a price target of $63, saying that he believes the company is "positioned to capitalize on long-term opportunities in oilfield activity globally triggered by the ongoing disruptions and shifting supply dynamics in the Middle East."

The five-star analyst expects SLB's dominant position in the international oilfield services market to bolster its earnings power over the long term, supported by increased activity levels over the medium to long term.

Given management's commentary on accelerated exploration activity in regions such as Latin America, Africa and Asia, and his expectation for accelerated final investment decisions in deepwater projects in West Africa, the Gulf of America and Brazil, Mehta expects SLB to benefit from higher services activity needed amid increasing drilling and production.

Furthermore, Mehta expects portfolio diversification from the Digital business and data center growth to drive higher earnings over the long term. Notably, the analyst expects SLB to deliver margins of about 40% in the Digital business this year, with further expansion in the years ahead.

Mehta ranks No. 626 among more than 12,300 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 60% of the time, delivering an average return of 10.7%. See SLB AI Stock Analysis on TipRanks.

Finally, moving on to tech giant IBM (IBM). The company is increasingly focusing on quantum computing and artificial intelligence to drive future growth. At a quarterly dividend of $1.69 per share, IBM stock offers a dividend yield of 2.7%.

Following a fireside chat with Ric Lewis, senior vice president of infrastructure at IBM, Bank of America analyst Wamsi Mohan reaffirmed a buy rating on IBM stock and increased his price target to $315 from $300.

The five-star analyst noted that Lewis views IBM Infrastructure as an increasingly less cyclical and more structurally advantaged business, with AI driving additional demand across the entire technology stack rather than only in graphics processing units.

Mohan added that AI tailwinds are most evident in IBM's Z mainframe offering, where program-to-program growth has increased from 110% several generations ago to the range of 120% to 125% in the prior cycle and roughly 135% for Z17. This acceleration is driven by AI workloads moving beyond fraud detection into inferencing areas like insurance, actuarial modeling, and transaction-level intelligence.

The analyst noted that IBM is benefiting from customers upgrading their systems and increased revenue from higher-value workloads from its existing customer base. Mohan also noted other positives like AI-led demand in IBM's storage business and the quantum roadmap.

"Overall, the fireside reinforced that IBM's Infrastructure business is positioned to compound through a combination of accelerating Z demand, AI-driven workload expansion, storage strength, and better monetization across a differentiated full-stack architecture," said Mohan.

Mohan ranks No. 21 among more than 12,300 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 65% of the time, delivering an average return of 52.6%. See IBM Insider Trading Activity on TipRanks.

#3216. Nexo Card data shows its European users spend twice the euro-area average

European Nexo Card holders spent about €80 per transaction in 2025, roughly double the euro-area card average. Nearly a third went on travel, eating out and leisure.

A long lunch with a colleague. A wellness class after work. A weekend away, booked from the sofa before bed. The purchases look ordinary. The money behind them does not.

According to Nexo’s new report, Digital assets and the European lifestyle, European Nexo cardholders spent about €80 per transaction in 2025. That is roughly double the euro-area card average of around €38 recorded by the European Central Bank for the second half of 2025. The findings draw on anonymised, aggregated Nexo Card transaction data across the European Economic Area from 1 January to 31 December 2025.

The headline is not that crypto holders spend differently. It is that they spend on the same things as everyone else, with bigger tickets. And they fund it in a way traditional cards cannot.

Nearly a third of all Nexo Card spending went on travel, eating out and leisure. That roughly matches all other retail spending combined once groceries are set aside. Restaurants alone took 88.5% of food and drink spending.

Travel was the card’s second-largest category, at 15.9% of volume. That fits the setting. Europe captured about $2 trillion of the $6.15 trillion spent on leisure travel worldwide in 2025, according to the World Travel & Tourism Council.

And the card is not reserved for special occasions. For more than half of cardholders, it also paid for the weekly grocery shop.

Compared with 2024, spending on the Nexo Card rose fastest in the categories that shape a lifestyle:

The Nexo Card works in two modes. In credit mode, clients borrow against holdings such as Bitcoin and Ether instead of selling them. In debit mode, the card converts digital assets at the point of sale.

When clients pay directly with crypto, stablecoins dominate. 72.7% of that spending goes through assets designed to hold a steady value, although that stability is not guaranteed.

“What the data shows is a European consumer who spends on everyday categories, with higher ticket sizes,” said Yasen Yankov, Head of Product Management at Nexo. “We see digital asset wealth, made spendable by tools like the Nexo Card, becoming a new driver of consumption.”

The spending sits on top of a widening base of ownership. In early 2026, about one in five respondents in the Netherlands and one in six in Germany said they owned crypto assets, according to the Adan and Ipsos 2026 Barometer. In France, 53% of holders had already paid for something with crypto, most often by card.

The missing piece, Nexo argues, has been infrastructure: tools that let people use their assets without selling them, turning stored wealth into everyday spending.

Alongside the report, Nexo announced that its card is now available in several overseas territories and autonomous regions of EU countries, many of them popular travel destinations:

Nexo describes its card, which runs on the Mastercard network, as the first crypto card to combine credit and debit functions.

Payments infrastructure rarely makes headlines. People notice the dinner, the flight and the spa day, not the rails underneath. A year of Nexo Card data suggests that for a growing group of Europeans, those rails are now partly built on digital assets.

#3215. Apple reportedly met with Thai officials over spyware alerts sent to politicians

Bloomberg reports that Apple has met with Thai government officials in the wake of its recent wave of iPhone alerts about mercenary spyware attacks. Here are the details.

Last week, The Financial Times and TechCrunch reported that Apple had sent a fresh wave of threat notifications to potential spyware targets in 99 countries, warning them that they may have been targeted by mercenary spyware attacks.

At the time, the FT focused on German lawmakers who had received the warnings, while TechCrunch highlighted recipients in other countries, including Beirut-based filmmaker Radwan Mortada.

Today, Bloomberg reported that “Thailand held meetings with Apple Inc. officials” over the notifications, adding that the warnings raised questions about “who may have targeted [Thai politicians] and why.”

Receiving an alert doesn’t necessarily mean a device was successfully compromised, Digital Economy and Society Minister Chaichanok Chidchob said after meeting Apple representatives Wednesday, Krungthep Turakij and other media reported. Thai authorities also have no evidence so far that the latest attempted attacks involved Pegasus, the spyware developed by Israel’s NSO Group, he said.

As Bloomberg explains, Pegasus was “allegedly used against pro-democracy campaigners in 2022.”

The recent wave of alerts, which were sent out on October 29, followed another round in August, when Apple notified potential targets in 110 countries. As always, Apple declined to disclose what triggers these notifications to prevent attackers from evading detection in the future, but recommended that recipients enable Lockdown Mode and seek expert security assistance.

Bloomberg added that Thai authorities are expected to meet with other technology companies on Thursday to discuss potential countermeasures, including risks to Android devices.

#3214. I tested Lenovo's Yoga 9n 2-in-1 against the MacBook Pro for two weeks — impressive OLED and AI smarts cannot make up for poor gaming and weaker raw power

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

Unlock and manage exclusive Tom’s Guide member rewards.

Join the Tom's Guide Club for quick access. Enter your email below and we'll send confirmation, and sign you up to our newsletter.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Lenovo Yoga 9n 2-in-1 impressed me with its beautiful OLED touchscreen, versatile design and local AI performance. However, its high price, disappointing gaming performance and weaker raw processing power make it difficult to recommend over a MacBook Pro. It's a promising showcase for Nvidia's RTX Spark platform, but not quite the MacBook replacement I hoped for.

Beautiful design with versatile 2-in-1 functionality

Bright, vibrant OLED touchscreen with included pen

Impressive local AI performance thanks to CUDA cores

Smooth everyday productivity and multitasking

Raw creative performance trails high-end MacBooks

Gaming performance isn't great for the price

Battery life falls short of MacBook standards

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

You've probably heard the term "MacBook killer," especially following the launch of Nvidia's first RTX Spark laptops. Now, Apple has raised the stakes with its latest MacBook Pro models featuring the PROLED XDR Displays, and I wanted to see how these new machines actually stack up.

So, I put my 16-inch MacBook Pro M3 Max away for two weeks and used the Lenovo Yoga 9n 2-in-1 as my only laptop. I wanted to find out whether Nvidia's new platform could replace an older MacBook Pro, how it compares with Apple's latest flagships, and what makes RTX Spark laptops worth considering.

The Yoga makes a strong impression. Its versatile design, vibrant OLED touchscreen, and support for local AI workloads give me plenty to like. But after two weeks, I found that while it's a capable everyday laptop, its high price and performance trade-offs make it a more specialized alternative to a MacBook rather than a true replacement.

Nvidia  RTX Spark N1X with 5120-core GPU and 18-core CPU

Nvidia RTX Spark N1X 6144 Core GPU, 20-Core NPU

Nvidia RTX Spark N1X 6144 Core Blackwell GPU

2x USB-A, 2x USB-C, 1x HDMI 2.1, 1x 3.5mm Headphone jack, 1x SD card slot

2x USB-A, 2x USB-C, 1x HDMI 2.1, 1x 3.5mm Headphone jack, 1x SD card slot

This Lenovo Yoga 9n 2-in-1 is a versatile machine. It features a 360-degree hinge for tablet use, pen support, and a striking design with speaker grilles flanking the screen and keyboard.

Tent mode is perfect for sitting on my sofa and streaming episodes of “King of the Hill.” Folding the screen flat lets me use the giant 16-inch display as a primary monitor in the lab at work with an external keyboard and mouse.

Of course, holding a 16-inch screen like a tablet can feel a bit unwieldy. However, the ability to use the included pen in photo-editing apps like Photoshop is a nice feature. I also give Lenovo credit for including a pen in the box. There's even a small cradle that magnetically attaches to the top of the laptop, so you don't have to worry about losing the stylus.

The Yoga’s “Ice Blue" finish and polished accents also give this laptop a glamorous look, making it feel like a jewel on my desk. My Space Black MacBook just looks plain and boring compared to this Yoga 9n.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

The keyboard and touchpad are also excellent. The dedicated number pad makes spreadsheet work far easier than on my MacBook, while the haptic touchpad matches Apple's gold standard. Clicks feel crisp, and special Windows-specific feedback for actions like closing windows and completing file transfers adds a nice tactile touch that my Mac lacks.

You can even use the pen on the haptic touchpad instead of writing directly on the screen. It can feel a bit strange, but it's another example of the flexibility this design offers. I could never imagine Apple doing that on a Mac.

Connectivity is another area where the Yoga has an advantage over my MacBook. In addition to HDMI and a full-size SD card reader, Lenovo includes two USB-A ports, which you won't find on a modern MacBook Pro.

Given the laptop's relatively thick 0.69-inch chassis and 4.28-pound weight, there's plenty of room for extra connections. During my two weeks with the Yoga, I left my dongles at home, which was a surprisingly refreshing change.

One of the biggest reasons I enjoy using the Yoga 9n 2-in-1 is the 16-inch OLED touchscreen. It's large, colorful, and bright enough to make everything from productivity work to streaming video enjoyable.

However, there's a new challenger in town. Apple's latest MacBook Pro, with its PROLED XDR display, has raised the bar for what we expect from a laptop screen. Although the numbers show that the Yoga 9n 2-in-1 doesn't quite match Apple's latest MacBook, that doesn't make it any less good.

Its 16-inch size gives me plenty of room to multitask with Google Chrome tabs and Slack while working in the lab. Brightness also reaches just over 1,000 nits in HDR, and one of my favorite shows, "King of the Hill," looks incredibly vibrant.

The episode where Bobby dresses up as the local college's mascot to help out Connie was a particularly good showcase. The oranges and other rich colors in the mascot suit practically jumped off the screen, making the animation look wonderfully alive.

In our lab tests, the Yoga's panel delivered a particularly high and oversaturated color volume, measuring 193.1% sRGB and 136.6% DCI-P3. It also ranked third in SDR brightness among the MacBook Pro 16-inch with M5 Max, Galaxy Book 6 Ultra, and HP Omnibook Ultra 16, reaching 449.8 nits and delivering an impressive 1,002 nits in HDR. Its 0.30 Delta-E result also placed it fourth in color accuracy among the laptops we compared.

However, the MacBook Pro 16-inch M5 Max PROLED XDR still comes out ahead in several important areas. It ranks first in brightness, reaching 549 nits in SDR and an impressive 1,949 nits in HDR. It also delivers the best color accuracy with a near-perfect 0.19 Delta-E.

However, Yoga is a more compelling matchup against my MacBook Pro M3 Max. As shown in the photo above, Lenovo's display produced particularly striking colors in the individual feathers of a parrot. Still, Apple's OLED display delivered more natural-looking detail and contrast, which I ultimately preferred.

Apple has also introduced touchscreen support on its new MacBook Pro and macOS, giving the Yoga serious competition in this category. If you're simply looking for the best touchscreen OLED laptop, Apple's latest MacBook Pro is hard to beat. However, choosing the MacBook means giving up the Yoga's 2-in-1 versatility and included pen.

Considering that the two laptops cost roughly the same in the configurations I tested, your choice will largely come down to pen support and whether you prefer Apple's ecosystem or Lenovo's more flexible design.

RTX Spark-powered laptops like this one aren’t really mainstream. They are more specialized notebooks focused on running local AI and taking advantage of native CUDA cores and the unified memory setup in this new chip from Nvidia. This makes them more of a laptop for developers and those who might want to run local agent platforms.

I tested this myself by downloading LM Studio and loading the Qwen 3.8-27b model. I took the Yoga 9n 2-in-1 offline and asked the model to write a 30-chapter novel about an earthquake in NYC and to describe the government falling apart and the city descending into chaos. The model produced an answer in 6 minutes and 20 seconds.

My final project for a college creative writing class was similar, so I was especially interested in seeing what the local model could produce. The chapters were relatively short and didn't include nearly as much detail as my own writing, yet the model still produced a coherent story. I was impressed by how much it could accomplish entirely on the laptop without an internet connection.

Out of curiosity, I also ran UL Procyon’s Text Gen benchmark. Across all the workloads, it scored 2,635, 2,346, 2,274, and 2,148. This was with the Phi-3.5-mini, Mistral 7B, Llama-3.1-8B, and Llama-2-13B LLM instruct models using CUDA acceleration.

We don’t run these tests on every Windows laptop and Mac, so I have no reference to compare them to, but those numbers look great. According to UL’s own scoring page, scores are in the lower 200s for Intel Core Ultra chips and in the 1,000s for Snapdragon X2 Elite chips. This shows that this first-gen ARM chip from Nvidia is in a great place for AI performance.

For now, the most compelling reason to buy an RTX Spark laptop is its ability to run local AI workloads. That's a much more specialized use case than everyday productivity or gaming, and it's something worth considering before spending this much on a laptop.

The Yoga 9n 2-in-1 isn't designed to be a conventional productivity laptop. Nvidia's RTX Spark platform places a strong emphasis on AI, but that doesn't mean you can't use it for everyday work, creative applications, or even gaming.

For my typical laptop workload, the Yoga is more than capable. I regularly juggle Chrome tabs, Slack, and other applications while working in the lab, and I have no major issues keeping everything running smoothly. Photoshop works well for photo editing, and I have no trouble using Wondershare Filmora on Windows 11.

In other words, for everyday tasks, the Yoga 9n 2-in-1 was a perfectly capable replacement for my MacBook. The raw performance benchmark results, however, tell a different story and are a downside of this laptop.

For raw processing power, the Yoga 9n 2-in-1 struggles to justify its premium price. I give Nvidia credit for delivering competitive performance from its first-generation Arm chip. However, there's still a noticeable gap in demanding creative applications.

The MacBook Pro 16-inch M5 Max PROLED XDR outperformed Lenovo’s laptop across our major productivity and creative benchmarks, with particularly large leads in Geekbench 6 and Premiere Pro.

The Yoga scored 13,437 in Photoshop and 85,779 in Premiere Pro. Apple's MacBook Pro was also considerably faster in both, completing the test in 7,75 minutes in Photoshop and 4,47 minutes in Premiere Pro.

Lenovo Yoga 9n 2-in-1 (RTX Spark, 64GB RAM)

MacBook Pro 16-inch M5 Max PROLED XDR (M5 Max, 128GB RAM)

HP OmniBook Ultra 16 (RTX Spark, 32GB RAM)

In Geekbench 6, the Yoga scored 3,076 single-core and 20,084 multi-core. That's ahead of the Samsung Galaxy Book 6 Ultra (2,852 and 16,655) and puts it almost neck and neck with the HP OmniBook Ultra 16, which has RTX Spark (3,165 / 20,056). However, the MacBook Pro M5 Max remains considerably ahead at 4,359 single-core and 30,327 multi-core.

The results are particularly interesting when comparing the Yoga against my older 16-inch MacBook Pro M3 Max. Apple's previous-generation high-end chip scored 3,162 in Geekbench 6 single-core and 21,250 in multi-core. While the Yoga comes surprisingly close, it still falls behind. Its HandBrake result of 2:00, however, comfortably beats my older MacBook's 2:37.

The takeaway is that Nvidia's first-generation RTX Spark platform delivers solid everyday performance and competitive results in certain creative workloads. However, the Yoga doesn't consistently outperform newer high-end, near-fully specced-out MacBooks, making it harder to justify spending $3,999 if raw processing power is your priority.

Gaming and Nvidia go hand in hand, and this Yoga can certainly run demanding games. However, RTX Spark isn't a ticket to high-end gaming performance. Developers need to optimize their games for the new Arm-based architecture, or the games won't run at all. That's why I found out that some games from our lab's catalog (like Red Dead Redemption 2) won’t run at all. Others, like Far Cry 6, also misbehaved and didn’t run properly.

I technically can't play Forza Horizon 6 on my MacBook, so the Yoga still has the edge for my gaming needs. I enjoyed playing it with extreme settings and ray tracing enabled, and it averaged 38 frames per second at 1080p. Increasing the resolution dropped it to 23 fps, though. That's playable, but hardly the kind of performance you’d expect from a $3,999 laptop.

Assassin’s Creed Shadows (Medium, 1080p, 1880p)

Cyberpunk 2077 (Ray Tracing Ulta, 1080p, 1880p)

The results are more mixed in other games. In Cyberpunk 2077, the Yoga managed 34.55 fps at 1080p with Ray Tracing Ultra enabled, putting it in the same general range as the other laptops we tested. At higher resolution, it actually outperforms the MacBook and Samsung, although the HP was slightly ahead. Assassin's Creed Shadows is less impressive, with the Yoga reaching just 25 fps at 1080p.

Our synthetic benchmarks tell a similar story. In 3DMark Wild Life Extreme, the Yoga scored 21,830, averaging 130.21 fps. That's slightly behind the HP OmniBook Ultra 16, which scored 22,978 and averaged 137 fps.

Compared to a MacBook, the Yoga can game, but these results put it closer to an RTX 5070 gaming laptop. It won’t be a compelling choice if gaming is your main priority. You can get a more capable gaming laptop for this kind of money.

The top reason I love my MacBook Pro is its battery life, since I only have to charge it at most three times a week. When I tried to replace my Mac with the Yoga 9n 2-in-1, I quickly learned that this system can’t match what my MacBook Pro delivers. Even lab results show that this Yoga is behind the competition.

I put the Yoga 9n 2-in-1 through my daily workflow and started the day fully charged. With the screen at a comfortable 33% brightness, I worked through spreadsheets in Google Sheets, talking to my coworkers on Slack, and taking the occasional Google Meet meeting. By the time 3:30 got around, the battery was down to 62%. That was more than enough for when I got home, but after two hours of watching YouTube videos and cartoons on Hulu, I got the recharge warning and had to plug the laptop into power.

In our lab tests, MacBook Pro 16-inch (M5 Max PROLED XDR) claims first place with a marathon runtime of 21:24, followed in second by the Samsung Galaxy Book 6 Ultra at a solid 15:11. The Lenovo Yoga 9i 2-in-1 takes third place with 12:20, leaving the HP OmniBook Ultra 16 (RTX Spark) in fourth at 10:52.

Lenovo’s RTX Spark 2-in-1 is ahead of HP’s, but the numbers don’t lie: the Yoga 9n isn’t the best for battery life.

Lenovo’s Yoga 9n 2-in-1 is an expensive proposition. As configured, our unit costs $3,999 directly from Lenovo. The same configuration is slightly cheaper at Best Buy for $3,749.99. If you want to save money, you can also pick up the entry-level model with the N1X 18-Core Processor, 32GB RAM, and a 512GB SSD for $3,199.99 from Lenovo or $3,099 from Best Buy.

Those prices are pretty wild, but the ongoing RAM crisis and the tough economy are what contribute to them. Apple’s MacBooks are around the same price and, frankly, arguably deliver better performance.

You can get a 16-inch MacBook Pro with the NanoTexture PROLED XDR display, M5 Pro chip, 24GB RAM, and a 1TB SSD for $3,549.99. That’s still cheaper than the Yoga 9n 2-in-1. If you remove the nano-texture display, you can also upgrade to an M5 Max chip with an 18-core CPU, a 32-core GPU, 36GB RAM, and 2TB of storage for $4,799.99. That’s about $800 more than the Yoga, but you’d get more storage and a better screen.

The point is that these RTX Spark machines are not cheap. Most people shouldn’t consider buying them, since their use case is more specialized for AI than anything else. You can take that money and put it toward a brand-new MacBook Pro instead. Or, if you’re really on a budget, invest that $3,999 in a better Windows laptop like the Samsung Galaxy Book 6 Ultra, known for its OLED screen and battery life.

The Lenovo Yoga 9n 2-in-1 is an intriguing, beautifully built hybrid that serves as an impressive canvas for Nvidia’s RTX Spark platform. Thanks to a stunning 16-inch OLED touchscreen, included stylus, versatile 360-degree hinge, and local AI power, there is plenty to like. During my two weeks with it, the Yoga easily replaced my MacBook Pro for everyday productivity tasks like web browsing, Slack, and multimedia consumption.

However, at $3,999 as tested, it doesn't quite earn the title of "MacBook Killer." For heavy creative professionals, it might not be a strong enough MacBook replacement, given its weaker raw processing power in demanding benchmarks and rendering tasks. Likewise, due to its poor battery life, it simply didn't fit into my lifestyle the way my long-lasting Mac does.

If your daily workflow hinges on running local AI models on a flexible 2-in-1 canvas, the Yoga 9n will be for you. But for most power users seeking maximum performance and all-day endurance, a high-end MacBook Pro remains the smarter investment.
