Electronic products now pack circuits, structures, thermal paths, and packaging into very small spaces. These physical domains interact with one another. A packaging choice can change how a shock load reaches a circuit board. Such interactions are hard to predict. Most are found during physical qualification, late in development. At that stage, the design is mostly fixed. A failure leads to redesign, rebuilds, and retesting. Physical tests give strong evidence of robustness, but they give limited insight into load paths and failure margins. Traditional simulation gives more detail, but it needs specialist skills and long manual setup. This white paper explains how guided virtual validation brings shock and drop assessment into the design phase. It reviews common test configurations, model inputs, and acceptance criteria. A packaged drop case study then shows how packaging can be optimized across all drop orientations and checked against physical test results.

#3198. Top Wall Street analysts are bullish on these 3 stocks for strong long-term growth potential

Global stock markets have been volatile as investors continue to assess geopolitical risks in the Middle East, fundamentals and valuations of companies in the artificial intelligence (AI) market and key economic data.

Top Wall Street analysts help investors look past near-term noise and pick attractive stocks with solid long-term growth potential.

Here are three stocks favored by some of Wall Street's top pros, according to TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Credo Technology (CRDO) provides high-speed connectivity solutions for AI data centers. Robust AI-led demand for the company's copper and optical interconnects has boosted revenue, driving a solid year-to-date rally.

In his latest research report, Bank of America analyst Vivek Arya raised his price targets on major semiconductor and semiconductor capital equipment stocks, with the price target for CRDO jumping to $340 from $252 with a reiterated a buy rating.

The 5-star analyst noted that Credo is seeing continued strength in the demand for its AECs (active electrical cables) from major and emerging hyperscalers. Moreover, the company has additional growth opportunities in optical DSPs (digital signal processors), ZF optics, ALCs (active LED cables), and PCIe retimers. These products are expected to begin ramping up production and profits in 2027-2028.

Following a meeting with the company at the 2026 BofA Global Tech Conference, along with recent channel checks, Arya raised his sales outlook for Credo by 2%-11% for fiscal 2027-2028 and his earnings per share (EPS) outlook by 5%-15%. The improved estimates reflect a strong AEC market outlook over the next five years and the company's "bulletproof reliability and incremental nature of its optical portfolio."

Arya based his new price target on a price-to-earnings multiple of 34x 2028 earnings, compared to the prior valuation of 33x 2027 earnings, saying it reflects contributions from new product adoption in coming years.

Arya ranks No. 84 among more than 12,300 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 62% of the time, delivering an average return of 31.5%. See Credo Technology Statistics on TipRanks.

Next on this week's list is Facebook- and Instagram parent Meta Platforms (META). Recently, Meta introduced consumer and business paid subscription plans for its Family of Apps and a new suite of Meta One (AI) subscription offerings.

Following the launch, Evercore ISI analyst Mark Mahaney reiterated a buy rating on META with a price target of $930. Mahaney views the rollout of the new subscription plans as a revenue diversification initiative, which could have a modest impact on revenue and eventually an even greater impact on operating income.

The 5-star analyst explained that he doesn't expect these new offerings to significantly affect near-term revenue growth due to their phased rollout and potentially low initial conversion rates. But he believes that even modest adoption within Meta's massive user base (over 3.6 billion daily users) could evolve into a significant high-margin revenue stream over the long term.

Mahaney highlighted that META is among Evercore ISI's top three, large-cap long-term picks, alongside Amazon and Spotify. His channel checks remain positive on Meta. Moreover, Mahaney noted that the Mark Zuckerberg-led company is successfully using AI to enhance user and advertiser satisfaction, reflected in engagement and return on ad spend (ROAS).

"What we now have with Facebook, Instagram, and WhatsApp Plus subscriptions is another attractive greenfield monetization opportunity for Meta – one that is not captured in Street estimates," concluded Mahaney, adding that his 2028 revenue estimate is 5% above Wall Street's consensus projection.

Mahaney ranks No. 987 among more than 12,300 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 53% of the time, delivering an average return of 9.8%. See Meta Platforms Financials on TipRanks.

Another social media platform in this week's list is Pinterest (PINS). Guggenheim analyst Michael Morris recently reiterated a buy rating on PINS with a price target of $24, citing "continued usage health and strengthening U.S. advertising business, each supported by ongoing AI-powered improvements."

The 5-star analyst highlighted that Pinterest has delivered double-digit global user growth for ten consecutive quarters, with his May data analysis indicating particular momentum in the second quarter of 2026. Morris said his Q2 2026 revenue growth estimate is at the high end of the company's guidance range.

Notably, Morris expects double-digit top-line growth in the United States and Canada to continue as large retailers adapt to new tariffs and the company's heightened focus on mid-market/small- and medium business advertisers expands its revenue base.

Morris believes that the adoption of Pinterest's Performance+ AI-powered advertising offering remains a major growth catalyst, currently accounting for 30% of lower-funnel revenue. The analyst sees scope for further penetration of this tool as advertisers using the product are increasing spending at nearly twice the rate of non-users.

Furthermore, Morris believes that the tvScientific acquisition expands Pinterest's reach into connected TV advertising, expanding the value of the platform's users offsite. He expects tvScientific to add about 2 points to PINS' quarterly revenue growth through the rest of the year, given the impact of business's seasonality and its U.S.-only footprint.

Morris ranks No. 857 among more than 12,300 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 54% of the time, delivering an average return of 12.9%. See Pinterest Ownership Structure on TipRanks.

#3197. Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia CEO after 33 years, effective immediately

NVIDIA founder and CEO Jensen Huang at NVIDIA GTC 2026 in San Jose

Jensen Huang has resigned as Nvidia’s president, CEO, and board member, effective immediately, the company’s board announced today, ending a 33-year run in which he built the chipmaker he co-founded into the roughly $4T centrepiece of the AI boom.

Chief financial officer Colette Kress steps in as interim CEO while the board searches for a permanent successor, and Harvey C. Jones becomes the company’s first-ever board chair, a role Huang never relinquished until now.

“NVIDIA’s strength has always come from its people, and together with our leadership team, I am committed to building on the extraordinary foundation Jensen created over the last 33 years,” Kress said.

The resignation caps a two-week unravelling that began with reports that US intelligence believed Alice Huang, a Megaspeed executive with whom Huang had a relationship, was recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security to spy on him, per the New York Times.

Jensen Huang admitted in a memo to employees that he had been unfaithful to his wife, and on Sunday the board opened an independent investigation while expressing confidence in his leadership.

Yet, that confidence lasted four days, as on Wednesday the NYT reported a second relationship, with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of healthcare and one of his direct reports; the Wall Street Journal reported the company was preparing to fire him; and the board met late into the night without announcing a decision.

By Thursday morning in the US, Huang had resigned.

The market damage is already historic. Nvidia had shed roughly $600B in value since the investigation was announced, and the stock fell as much as 10% more on news of the resignation. The company reports quarterly earnings on November 17, its first ever without the leather-jacketed founder who fronted every one.

The board’s statement does not mention the allegations at all, thanking Huang instead for his “immeasurable contributions”.

He departs holding about 3.6% of the company, and leaves behind the succession vacuum he created: dozens of direct reports, no anointed heir, and an interim CEO drawn from finance rather than the technology roadmap.

Bloomberg reported this week that an outside firm is compiling candidates; prediction markets have favoured Ian Buck, who runs the data-centre business that supplies the AI industry.

Whoever gets the job inherits a company that is simultaneously the most valuable enterprise on Earth, the hinge of the US-China technology conflict, and, as of today, proof that no founder is bigger than his board.

#3195. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang set to be fired, with Johny Srouji among possible replacements [U]

Following reports of a potential second affair – this time with a subordinate – Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang looks certain to be fired by the company’s board, probably later today (though he may be allowed to ‘resign’). Apple’s chief hardware officer Johny Srouji has been listed among the potential replacements, though this seems unlikely.

Update: As we predicted, he’s gone today and Kress was indeed named interim CEO …

For anyone who’s been away from the planet for the past fortnight, Huang’s affair with a woman suspected to be a Chinese spy has been the main headline news in the tech press since it came to light at the end of last month. The New York Times broke the story on October 29, citing it then as “a close relationship.” Nvidia initially denied that the relationship was anything out of the ordinary.

That changed on November 8 when Huang publicly admitted to the affair. Nvidia’s shares dropped 5%, and the company’s board of directors opened an independent investigation. Further details emerged over the following days.

Things got even worse yesterday when the same paper reported that Huang had also had an affair with an Nvidia executive who reports to him.

It was already looking inevitable that he would be fired, and the latest revelation adds to the urgency. The Wall Street Journal reported that the board was meeting last night to discuss the CEO’s future. That future at Nvidia is likely to be measured in hours rather than days.

The board now needs to find a replacement, and Bloomberg provides a rundown on some of the potential candidates. CFO Colette Kress looks likely to head the list for at least an interim appointment. The paper names a number of other possibilities, including Apple’s chief hardware officer, Johny Srouji.

Srouji has led one of the most successful in-house silicon programs in the industry, overseeing the custom chips that power the iPhone, Mac and other Apple devices. His track record gives him deep credibility on chip design, product integration and long-term technology roadmaps. But much of his experience has been built inside Apple’s tightly controlled ecosystem, and he hasn’t been tested in the kind of high-profile salesmanship which Huang is famous for.

Given the urgency, my money is on Nvidia announcing Kress as at least interim CEO, if not a permanent replacement. It seems exceedingly unlikely that Srouji would be appointed at this time, given the in-depth negotiations and discussions that would need to take place.

As to whether he’s a potential candidate following an interim appointment, it still seems unlikely. There were earlier reports of his previous dissatisfaction at the company, but it seems a stretch to imagine him jumping ship so soon after his promotion to chief hardware officer.

#3194. 30% of iPhone Duo buyers may have returned it, but I don’t think Apple should worry

A poll of 9to5Mac readers who were lucky enough to take delivery of their iPhone Duo in the first few days shows that 30% of them have returned it for a refund.

While that could be considered bad news for the future of the device, I don’t personally consider it either surprising or worrying …

Following a report by The Verge on iPhone Duo buyers who opted to return the device for a refund within Apple’s 14-day “no questions asked” period, we thought it would be interesting to get a sense of how many people may have done this.

9to5Mac readers were always likely to have had their fingers hovering over the pre-order button for the best shot at taking early delivery, with the first of these having hit the end of the 14-day window. We ask those of you who fall into this category to tell us whether you kept or returned the device.

With close to 6,000 total votes, the results showed that close to a third of you returned your Duo.

For any other device, that would be a disastrous return rate. For the Duo, however, I don’t think it’s terribly surprising.

As we noted yesterday, Apple described the iPhone Duo as “the most transformational change to iPhone since the original.” The size of that change shows up in a whole range of ways, from the weight of the device through the changed aspect ratio of the front display to a completely new way of using an iPhone.

Throw in the extremely high price tag, and I’ve always suspected that a significant number of iPhone Duo buyers would be viewing it as an experiment rather than a committed purchase. Our own Ryan Christoffel is an example of that “try it and see” attitude. One week in, he’s reached an interim conclusion that it’s probably not for him.

For those who’ve decided to return it, a number of readers shared their reasons.

“Returned it – I can’t go back to Touch ID.”

“I want to like it, but I just can’t get there. It’s awkward, and the outside screen is way too small.”

“Returned it. Not for me. I do not want to open the phone every time I want a larger screen and Apple made the outer display much less usable than it should be with that silly permanent dock. I also use my phones left-handed.”

“During a vacation in Morocco, we spent a night camping in the Sahara Desert. I was extremely careful with the phone and tried to avoid using it in the sand altogether. However, on the second day, when I opened it inside the tent, I heard a crunching sound coming from the hinge. Sand had somehow gotten inside. I tried everything I could to clean it, but nothing worked. The inner display was still functioning perfectly, but the phone would no longer open all the way. Even worse, when I tried to close it, I had to force it shut.”

For me personally, it couldn’t be my only phone, given the priority I place on the device as a camera, but I am still lusting after it. Given the continued extended delivery times – with random checks showing shipping in late January – I don’t think Apple has much to worry about here.

#3190. We've Witnessed the Stock Market Do This 19 Times in 76 Years, and Equities Have Been Higher One Year Later 100% of the Time

Past events have a knack for forecasting the future on Wall Street.

This has shaped up as another stellar year for the iconic Dow Jones Industrial Average (^DJI +0.06%), benchmark S&P 500 (^GSPC -0.43%), and growth-focused Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC -0.92%). The artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure build-out, better-than-expected corporate earnings, and record S&P 500 share buybacks have collectively lifted all three stock indexes to several new highs.

But recent volatility also suggests that equities may be on shaky ground. Just two days after the midterm elections, on Nov. 5, the Nasdaq Composite logged its largest-ever single-day point decline (1,422 points).

While headwinds are clearly mounting on Wall Street, historical precedent offers a different take.

Election Day went, more or less, as the prediction markets had forecast. Democrats swept both houses of Congress, setting up a scenario in which few major spending bills will be signed into law from January 2027 through January 2029.

But there was one surprise on Election Night that clearly unnerved professional and everyday investors. Democrats flipped five governorships previously held by Republicans (with two races still uncalled by the Associated Press, as of Nov. 9), including in Texas, Ohio, and Georgia. These three states are critical to the AI data center build-out. Whereas President Donald Trump favors as little regulation as possible for AI, most Democratic lawmakers want to limit data center expansion and ramp up the vetting of large language models.

Gina Hinojosa may not be as bad for Texas data centers as it looks. Her plan asks for: no subsidies, union labor, no NDAs, and proof household power and water bills won't rise. Much of that is already underway: Amazon, Google, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, Oracle and xAI pledged in March to bring their own power and pay for transmission Microsoft pledged to pay full property taxes without seeking tax breaks Nvidia is working with Vistra, NextEra and Constellation on data centers that cut power use when the grid is strained

The stock market entered 2026 at its second-highest valuation in history. A market that's priced for perfection can ill afford a slowdown in the AI infrastructure build-out.

The ideological differences between President Trump and the Democrat-led Congress will likely also make debt-ceiling negotiations more challenging.

If the Dow, S&P 500, and Nasdaq Composite are to reach new highs, they'll have to climb the proverbial wall of worry.

Although no predictive tool can ever guarantee what the Dow, S&P 500, and Nasdaq Composite will do over the short term, some past events have a knack for foreshadowing the future. One, in particular, has a flawless track record, dating back to 1950.

According to data from Morgan Stanley (MS -0.37%), the S&P 500 has been higher at the six- and 12-month marks following each of the previous 19 midterm elections since 1950.

Carson Group's Chief Market Strategist Ryan Detrick also notes that November has been green for the S&P 500 100% of the time following midterm elections over the last 76 years.

S&P 500 is higher 6 and 12 months after every midterm election over the last 75 years 📈🤑🥳 https://t.co/N1Eu0fZDie

Despite all the pre- and post-election noise that investors have been attempting to digest, history shows that stocks consistently head higher after midterm elections, regardless of how the political puzzle pieces are arranged. This data serves as a good reminder that factors such as corporate operating results, capital-return programs, management decisions, and innovation matter far more in the grand scheme of things on Wall Street than the makeup of Congress over the next two years.

Will there be stock market hiccups in the second half of Trump's term? More than likely, yes.

But have the midterm elections materially changed the long-term outlook for equities? A resounding no.

In this regard, recommendations from top Wall Street analysts can provide useful insights and help identify dividend stocks backed by solid fundamentals and with attractive upside potential.

Here are three dividend-paying stocks that are highlighted by Wall Street's top pros, as tracked by TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Independent oil and natural gas company Permian Resources (PR) is this week's first dividend stock. The company recently paid a quarterly base cash dividend of 16 cents per share. At an annualized dividend of 64 cents per share, PR offers a dividend yield of 3.5%.

Recently, Evercore analyst Chris Baker initiated coverage of Permian Resources stock with a price target of $25. The analyst believes that the company is well positioned to benefit from improving U.S. shale demand after the Iran conflict, thanks to its low-breakeven inventory that can boost free cash flow growth. Baker also noted PR's disciplined consolidation in the Permian Basin.

Furthermore, the 5-star analyst highlighted the company's focus on a single basin and management's efficient capital allocations across expansion efforts, strategic acquisitions, and share buybacks. Baker noted that management focuses investments on the higher-return Northern Delaware Basin, helping boost profitability.

"The key piece of our work here, and the reason we think PR deserves a higher multiple relative to more finite or less flexible shale stories, is that PR runs an acquire and exploit model," said Baker.

He explained that Permian Resources deserves a premium valuation as it continually acquires and develops new high-quality assets instead of relying on a limited inventory, a strategy that is the market is underappreciating.

Baker ranks No. 862 among more than 12,300 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 75% of the time, delivering an average return of 48.3%. See Permian Resources Ownership Structure on TipRanks.

Valero Energy (VLO) is a manufacturer and marketer of petroleum-based and low-carbon liquid transportation fuels and petrochemical products. At a quarterly dividend of $1.20 per share, or annualized dividend of $4.80 per share, VLO stock offers a yield of about 2%.

Heading into Valero's second-quarter earnings on July 30, Goldman Sachs analyst Neil Mehta reiterated a buy rating on VLO stock and increased the price target to $286 from $283 to reflect updated estimates.

Specifically, the 5-star analyst raised his 2026 and 2027 earnings per share estimates to $31.42 and $23.07 from $29.42 and $21.06, respectively, while leaving the 2028 EPS estimate unchanged at $20.37. Mehta made these revisions based on several factors, including updated commodity price assumptions and changes to refining capture rates.

Despite a strong year-to-date rally in VLO stock, Mehta still finds it compelling due to his more positive refining outlook. Moreover, the analyst sees the possibility of solid estimate revisions, which could drive the stock higher. He believes that Valero is well-positioned to benefit from improving refining market conditions due to its strong position in the Gulf Coast, solid balance sheet strength, and low-cost operations.

"Additionally, we believe the company's premium asset portfolio and crude slate optionality should support capture rates and stronger cash flow generation in the near-term, ultimately supporting shareholder returns," said Mehta.

#3186. Great News for Nvidia, Micron, Broadcom, and AMD Stock Investors -- Wall Street Made a Mistake

Technology companies are investing in AI infrastructure much more aggressively than Wall Street analysts forecast earlier this year.

The semiconductor stocks listed below have created significant wealth for shareholders. The percentage next to each name quantifies the share price appreciation since January 2023.

All four stocks trade below their highs -- AMD is down 20%, Broadcom and Nvidia are down 30%, and Micron is down 40% -- but there is some good news for shareholders. AI spending will be much higher than Wall Street expected in 2026, and the same outcome is probable in 2027.

Wall Street analysts have consistently underestimated how much technology companies will spend on artificial intelligence infrastructure. According to JPMorgan Chase chief U.S. economist Michael Feroli, "The surge in AI -related expenditures has been the defining feature of our economic times."

In January, the consensus estimate said capital expenditures (capex) among the five largest hyperscalers -- Alphabet, Amazon, Meta Platforms, Microsoft, and Oracle -- would total $546 billion this year. But Wall Street now expects those companies to spend $800 billion in 2026, nearly double what they invested last year,

Similarly, the Wall Street consensus initially put capex spending at $630 billion in 2027, but that forecast has since been upwardly revised to $1.1 trillion. And Morgan Stanley expects spending to approach $1.6 trillion next year if CoreWeave, Nebius, and Space Exploration Technologies are included in the math.

So what? Wall Street analysts have dramatically raised their forecasts for AI infrastructure spending. Since January, the consensus capex forecasts for the top five hyperscalers have increased 50% for 2026 and 75% for 2027. Those are not minor revisions. They are major changes that reflect extraordinary demand.

Wall Street has now substantially underestimated hyperscaler capex spending in three consecutive years, which means the consensus forecasts for 2027 may be too low right now. That's good news for semiconductor companies Nvidia, AMD, Broadcom, and Micron.

Micron manufactures memory chips, including high-bandwidth memory (HBM), that are crucial in storing and delivering information to AI processors. Micron is the third-largest supplier of DRAM and NAND flash memory, behind Samsung and SK Hynix. Revenue increased 379% to $54. 2 billion last quarter, and the company should maintain its momentum as the AI boom creates more demand for memory and storage solutions.

Nvidia is best known for its graphics processing units (GPUs), powerful chips needed to train and run AI models. The company dominates the AI accelerator market, with over 80% revenue share, supported by its adjacent networking and software products. Revenue rose 106% to $96 billion in the last quarter, and Nvidia is well positioned for future growth due to the recent launch of its next-generation Vera Rubin platform.

Broadcom designs custom AI accelerator chips for six major technology companies, including OpenAI and Anthropic. It also dominates the market for data center switching and routing chips, with about 70% revenue share. Revenue increased 86% to $29.6 billion in the last quarter, and growth could accelerate if major customers lean more heavily on custom silicon as an alternative to Nvidia GPUs in the future.

AMD designs chips for personal computers and data centers, including GPUs that power AI applications. The company has taken substantial market share in central processing units (CPUs) from Intel in recent years, but it has failed to erode Nvidia's dominance in GPUs. Revenue increased 45% to $13.4 billion in the last quarter, but growth could accelerate as customers like OpenAI, Meta, and Microsoft seek alternatives to Nvidia GPUs.

For each company, the chart below lists the current price-to-earnings multiple and the Wall Street consensus for annual earnings growth over the next three years. It combines those numbers to find a price-to-earnings-to-growth (PEG) ratio.

As shown above, Micron is currently the cheapest of the four semiconductor stocks, with a PEG ratio of 0.2. Nvidia and Broadcom land in the middle. And AMD is the most expensive, with a PEG ratio of 1.6.

Interestingly, Wall Street analysts rank the stocks in the same order. The chart below shows the current share price, median target price, and implied upside for each.

Despite what Wall Street's forecasts imply, I think investors should purchase a position in all four stocks rather than attempt to pick one winner. Diversification is a smart move here. You never know what might go wrong for a single company -- recent headlines concerning Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang are proof of that.

#3185. Jensen Huang resigns as CEO of Nvidia

Jensen Huang has resigned as the CEO of Nvidia following recent reports of extramarital affairs, including one involving a woman suspected of spying for China. Here are the details.

In late October, The New York Times reported on Jensen Huang’s “close relationship” with Alice Huang, a former managing director at Singapore-based Megaspeed, whom US intelligence officials reportedly identified as a Chinese intelligence asset suspected of passing information to Beijing.

According to subsequent reports, Chinese intelligence allegedly recruited her to gather information about Jensen Huang and influence his position on selling advanced AI chips to Chinese companies. China disputes the espionage allegations, dismissing them as groundless speculation intended to smear the country.

That said, while Nvidia previously denied any impropriety in their relationship, Huang admitted last weekend to having an extramarital affair in a message to employees, saying, “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did.” He did not mention Alice Huang directly.

In the following days, concerns grew over the potential national security implications of the relationship, in addition to Nvidia seeing its stock plummet.

And while Huang remained CEO as Nvidia’s board commissioned an independent investigation into the allegations, The New York Times reported on Wednesday that he had a second extramarital affair, this time with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of healthcare, who reports directly to him.

In the hours that followed, The Wall Street Journal reported that Nvidia’s board was preparing to meet to decide Huang’s future. Soon after, Semafor reported that some board members favored Nvidia CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO, while other reports suggested that Huang’s daughter, Madison Huang, could eventually succeed him. Madison Huang works at Nvidia as senior director of product marketing.

Semafor also named Apple’s chief hardware officer, Johny Srouji, as a potential successor, while Bloomberg reported that Nvidia had hired an outside firm to identify candidates.

Now, Nvidia has officially announced that Huang “has resigned as President, Chief Executive Officer, and a member of the Board, effective immediately.”

The company confirmed that Kress has been appointed interim CEO, while retaining her current responsibilities, until a permanent successor is named. The company is considering both internal and external candidates.

Nvidia also announced that Harvey C. Jones, a longtime technology executive and venture investor, has been appointed the company’s first-ever board chair.

In a statement, Jones said the board has “full confidence in Colette and the leadership team,” adding that Nvidia expects its operations, customer commitments, and product roadmap to continue without interruption.

Nvidia did not directly address the allegations surrounding Huang in its announcement, instead thanking him for his contributions to the company over the past 33 years.

Following the Times’ Wednesday report, Nvidia shares plunged in after-hours trading, erasing the day’s 2.9% gain after two consecutive sessions of losses.

The stock continued to fall following today’s announcement, dropping more than 10% at the time of writing from Wednesday’s closing price of $173.73, bringing its total decline to approximately 35% from its October 6 record close.

How Nvidia’s stock will behave when the market opens today and in the days that follow is anyone’s guess, especially with the company scheduled to report its quarterly earnings next Tuesday, November 17.

#3183. Mount Thor raises $45 million to build Mac data centers for AI agents

Apple @ Work is exclusively brought to you by Mosyle, the only Apple Unified Platform. Mosyle is the only solution that integrates in a single professional-grade platform all the solutions necessary to seamlessly and automatically deploy, manage & protect Apple devices at work. Over 45,000 organizations trust Mosyle to make millions of Apple devices work-ready with no effort and at an affordable cost. Request your EXTENDED TRIAL today and understand why Mosyle is everything you need to work with Apple.

Mount Thor, a Bay Area startup building cloud infrastructure on Apple silicon, announced today that it has raised $45 million across Seed and Series A rounds. The pitch to its investors was simple: AI agents are incredible on Apple silicon, and nobody is renting them at data-center scale.

About Apple @ Work: Bradley Chambers managed an enterprise IT network from 2009 to 2021. Through his experience deploying and managing firewalls, switches, a mobile device management system, enterprise grade Wi-Fi, 1000s of Macs, and 1000s of iPads, Bradley will highlight ways in which Apple IT managers deploy Apple devices, build networks to support them, train users, stories from the trenches of IT management, and ways Apple could improve its products for IT departments.

CRV and Conviction co-led the Series A. Chad Byers and Offline Ventures co-led the Seed. CSC Leasing, Enea Capital, Long Journey Ventures, and Upper90 participated, along with angel investors from OpenAI, Meta, Cognition, Together AI, and Vercel. The company also raised separate non-dilutive financing for new hardware as well.

Mount Thor runs macOS on Apple silicon as elastic compute instances, just as a cloud provider rents Linux VMs. Customers get on-demand fleets of Macs for work that only happens on macOS: training computer-use models in reinforcement learning environments, running secure macOS sandboxes for agents, long-running instances that let an agent work across a user’s devices under one Apple ID, and build and test farms for Apple software.

There are two ways to use its solution. With managed compute, customers pick a machine class and image, and get either a full bare-metal Mac or an isolated macOS VM with administrator access, provisioned through a web portal, a command-line tool, Kubernetes, or the API, and billed per Mac on a 24-hour basis. With customer-managed compute, an organization runs its own Macs at a Mount Thor site using its own MDM, while Mount Thor operates the facility and provides inventory by serial number, problem reporting, and event notifications.

The argument is that agents are becoming macOS users, and the demand for Apple’s platform now scales with the number of agents rather than the number of people.

“Making Apple’s operating system and silicon available at datacenter-scale is a massive untapped opportunity in AI infrastructure,” said Peter Voell, Founder and CEO of Mount Thor. “Decades of investment in accessibility and human-computer interaction make macOS the best place for agents to work and for humans to hold them accountable. And with chips like the M5 Ultra, Apple silicon is becoming a high performance, more power- and cost- efficient platform for production inference.”

The other half of its pitch is inference. The M5 Ultra Mac Studio shipped in August with up to 512GB of unified memory, which puts large open-weight models within reach of a single machine at a fraction of the power draw of a traditional GPU-based server. Mount Thor says a focus of the new funding is building what it calls the best inference lab for open-source models on Apple silicon.

“Mount Thor sits at the intersection of two important shifts: the rapidly expanding capabilities of autonomous agents and the increasing demand for compute that can support both local and cloud workloads,” said Brittany Walker, General Partner at CRV. “We’re thrilled to back Peter and the team as they make it easier to use Apple’s platforms at scale for agentic AI.”

The team comes from Cerebras, CoreWeave, Fluidstack, Nebius, OpenAI, and xAI. The company was founded this year and deployed its first data center in under six months.

Macs in the cloud are not new as AWS has rented Mac instances for a few years, and MacStadium has been doing so longer than AWS. Mount Thor’s pitch is that the larger customer is an AI agent that needs a Mac to do its job, and that demand grows with the number of agents rather than the number of developers.

The company says the funding will go toward expanding its compute footprint and building out the team, and that it plans to add capacity quickly to keep up with customer demand.

#3182. Speech Processing Pioneer Bishnu Saroop Atal Dies at 93

IEEE also bids farewell to innovators in space, power, and telecom

Bishnu Saroop Atal received the 2013 IEEE Jack S. Kilby Signal Processing Medal for “fundamental and pioneering contributions to speech coding.”

Bishnu Saroop AtalAcoustics and signal processing pioneerLife Fellow, 93; died 19 August

Atal was an acoustics and signal processing researcher at Bell Labs in Murray Hill, N.J., and later at AT&T’s Shannon Laboratory, in Florham Park, N.J. His pioneering work on voice-coding techniques became the foundation for efficient, high-quality voice transmission over cellular networks. He received the 2013 IEEE Jack S. Kilby Signal Processing Medal for “fundamental and pioneering contributions to speech coding.”

He joined Bell Labs in 1961 as a communications researcher, and his early work there focused on speaker identification technology. During the 1960s he helped develop linear predictive coding, a powerful method for analyzing and compressing speech. LPC is now the most widely used method for encoding speech at a low bit rate.

Atal developed increasingly sophisticated low-bit-rate speech-coding techniques. They included multipulse LPC, which improved the quality of compressed speech.

He also worked with his colleague Manfred R. Schroeder to develop code-excited linear prediction, a method for producing high-quality speech at very low bit rates. CELP became a foundational technique in modern speech coding, letting digital communications systems carry voice using less bandwidth. The extra efficiency expanded cellular capacity, allowing wireless networks to handle more simultaneous calls.

Later in his career, he led the acoustics and speech research departments at Bell.

The company named him a Fellow in 1994. When AT&T Bell Laboratories split into separate research organizations in 1996, Atal continued his career at the AT&T Florham Park headquarters, and he was named a Fellow the following year.

He retired in 2002 and became an affiliate professor of electrical engineering at the University of Washington, in Seattle. There he continued his research in speech processing, speech recognition, and high-dimensional computing.

Atal was elected to the National Academy of Engineering in 1987 and the National Academy of Sciences in 1993. He received numerous awards including the 2018 International Speech Communication Association Medal for Scientific Achievement and a 2003 medal from the Franklin Institute.

He received a bachelor’s degree in physics in 1952 from the University of Lucknow, in India, and a master’s degree in 1955 in electrical engineering from the Indian Institute of Science, in Bengaluru. While working full time at Bell he earned a Ph.D. in EE in 1968 from the Polytechnic Institute of Brooklyn (now New York University’s Tandon engineering school), in New York City.

Darryl Palmer Jr.Chair of the IEEE Central Illinois SectionSenior member, 55; died 30 August

Palmer was a dedicated IEEE volunteer, serving as chair of the Central Illinois Section and as the government relations chair of Region 4. He was a member of the IEEE Industrial Electronics Society and its industrial activity committee. He also served as associate editor of the IEEE Transactions on Industrial Informatics.

In 1986, at age 16, Palmer completed a summer internship at NASA’s Glenn Research Center, in Cleveland. He helped develop FoilSim, an interactive educational software program that introduces aerodynamic engineering to preuniversity students.

While studying computer science at Cleveland State University in 1996, he joined the university’s Allen-Bradley PLC lab as a research assistant. He designed hardware and software systems for the Glenn Research Center to collect and process thermal wave imaging data. He also designed software for General Motors’ North American robotic and welding division.

In 1999 he completed a second internship at the research center and helped develop EngineSim, an educational software program that models jet engine design and testing.

For his work, NASA recognized him with a Space Act Award.

In 2000 he earned his bachelor’s degree in computer science and became a software engineer at the Danfoss Drives manufacturing facility in Loves Park, Ill. He worked on embedded control systems for variable-frequency drives and high-power equipment. He also developed sensorless control technology for beam pumps used in the oil and gas industry.

In 2014 Palmer and his wife, Alexandra “Sasha” Goodwin, founded Janus Choice, a health technology platform that matches hospital patients with post-acute care facilities. He served as its CEO until the company closed in 2020.

From 2018 to 2023, he was a lead software engineer at Adept Coalescence, a startup in Rockford, Ill., focused on developing front-end software for control systems. He then worked in Peoria, Ill., as a control systems team lead at Caterpillar, a manufacturer of construction and mining equipment.

Henry Leopold RichterTelecommunications engineerLife senior member, 99; died 12 August

Richter was a spacecraft engineer at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory, in Pasadena, Calif., before starting his own public safety communications consultancy.

He earned a bachelor’s degree and a Ph.D. at Caltech in 1952 and 1956, respectively. In 1955 he joined JPL as an engineer and supervisor of its new circuit elements group. Later, he was assigned to NASA’s Explorer program as project manager for satellite design, serving as a liaison between the organization’s satellite instrumentation group and its operations and data groups. Since 1958 the program has launched more than 90 missions for physics, geophysics, and astrophysics research.

As NASA prepared to launch Explorer 1 in January 1958, Richter worked with the San Gabriel Valley Radio Club in Los Angeles to set up stations across the United States to track the satellite.

He eventually was named JPL section chief and was responsible for scientific instruments on the lunar Ranger, Surveyor, and Mariner programs. He also helped develop NASA’s Deep Space Network, an international tracking and communications system.

Richter left NASA to become vice president and technical director of Xerox Electro-Optical Systems, in Pasadena, Calif.

In the mid-1970s, he joined the Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department as a communications engineer, overseeing the department’s microwave and mobile radio networks.

He later ran a telecommunications consulting practice for more than 20 years. His clients included federal, state, and local government agencies, school districts, universities, and organizations. His work covered strategic technology planning and the design and implementation of public safety radio, microwave, CCTV, and paging systems.

He wrote several books including America’s Leap Into Space: My Time at JPL and the First Explorer Satellites (2015), a personal account of his experience working on the Explorer 1 and America’s space program.

In 2019 the Radio Club of America presented him with its Lifetime Achievement Award for “significant achievements and a major body of work that has advanced the art and science of wireless technology.”

Raymond L. GiordanoFormer RCA engineerLife member, 91; died 19 July

Giordano was an electrical engineer who designed integrated circuits and defense electronics at companies including Harris, Intersil, and RCA.

After earning his bachelor’s degree in electrical engineering in 1956 from the Newark College of Engineering (now the New Jersey Institute of Technology), Giordano joined RCA in Moorestown, N.J., as an engineer. He helped develop a video formatter for the company’s missile and surface radar division, and he taught in-house engineering courses, eventually attaining the rank of senior technical staff member.

Later he developed technologies for General Electric (which acquired RCA in 1986), Intersil, and Harris. He designed the circuitry for Kodak’s Cameo cameras and one of its laser printers.

Giordano was awarded several patents for his designs including a smoke detector chip for Siemens, a speed control chip for Ford, an engine control system for Delco Remy, and a control component for Chrysler.

He earned a master’s degree in EE in 1964 from the University of Pennsylvania, in Philadelphia.

Delano D. WilsonPresident of Power TechnologiesLife Fellow, 92; died 26 May

Wilson was president and CEO of Power Technologies, a consulting firm in Schenectady, N.Y., that specialized in electric power systems.

He was a director of R&D at General Electric in Schenectady until he joined Power Technologies in 1974 as a principal engineer. He developed utility systems and software for the company.

Wilson authored six books and 65 technical papers, and he held two patents.

Outside of his engineering work, he served on the boards of several hospitals, YMCAs, Rotary clubs, and chambers of commerce.

After returning to his hometown of Great Falls, Mont., in 1995, he volunteered as a court-appointed advocate, a trained community volunteer appointed by a judge to represent the interests of children in foster care.

Daniel I. Amey Jr.Electronic packaging engineerLife Fellow, 84; died 12 March

Amey was an electronic packaging engineer, working at several companies including General Dynamics, Sperry Univac, and E.I. du Pont de Nemours (now DuPont). His research interests included connectors, chip packages, and high-frequency materials.

He began his career in 1963 as an engineer in the General Dynamics electronics division, where he designed military electronic hardware including analog and digital support equipment for aerospace applications.

In 1967 he joined Sperry Univac in Blue Bell, Pa. From 1972 to 1981 he was engineering manager of packaging techniques, responsible for interconnection hardware for small and medium computer systems. His work focused on large-scale integration packages, hybrid circuits, connectors, and printed wiring board processes.

He left the company to serve as director of electronics technology at Thomas & Betts of Raritan, N.J. He led research and development of packaging and interconnection products there.

In 1986 he became a director of Elco, an electrical component manufacturer in Huntingdon, Pa., where he was responsible for the design and development of connector and packaging hardware.

In 1988 he joined E.I. du Pont de Nemours as director of its electronics and communications technology group in Research Triangle Park, N.C. He worked on packaging technology development, high-frequency materials characterization, and applications engineering. He retired from there as a research fellow.

Amey wrote or cowrote more than 70 technical papers and held more than 14 patents. He developed courses on electronic packaging and printed wiring technology for education companies McGraw-Hill and Cobblestone (formerly the Center for Professional Advancement).

He received the International Microelectronics Assembly and Packaging Society’s 2004 Wagnon Technical Achievement Award and the Electronic Industries Association’s 1984 Distinguished Engineering Contribution Award.

After receiving a bachelor’s degree in electrical engineering and a master’s degree in engineering science from Pennsylvania State University, he earned an MBA from Lehigh University, in Bethlehem, Pa.

Amanda Davis is a freelance writer based in San Diego.

#3181. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigns live updates — Colette Kress named interim CEO and latest news

Join the Tom's Guide Club for quick access. Enter your email below and we'll send confirmation, and sign you up to our newsletter.

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

Unlock and manage exclusive Tom’s Guide member rewards.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

CEO and co-founder of Nvidia, Jensen Huang, has resigned in a decision that will send reverberations around the tech industry. Nvidia and the FBI have both launched investigations after Huang admitted to an affair with a suspected Chinese spy.

Huang has been pivotal in growing Nvidia into a $4 trillion juggernaut at the center of the current AI boom. The company operates a flat structure with no second-in-command. Nvidia stock already dropped 4% in overnight trading following the reveal of the affair and then fell even further after the New York Times reported Huang had a second extramarital relationship with an Nvidia employee called Kimberly Powell.

Now that Huang has confirmed his resignation we we'll be following the fallout live.

In 2025, US intelligence officials briefed Donald Trump regarding Jensen Huang’s close relationship with Alice Huang (no relation). Huang is an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data center company. US officials began watching her under the suspicion she’s smuggling Nvidia’s AI chips into China.

Spring 2026: A memo drafted by U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio circulates among top policymakers in the Trump administration — explicitly stating that the Megaspeed executive is a spy for China’s Ministry of State Security.

In May 2026, despite these concerns being circulated regarding Huang’s relationship with a suspected Chinese asset, he was invited to join Trump’s official delegation during a diplomatic trip to China.

At September’s White House State Dinner, Jensen Huang and his wife, Lori Huang, attended the dinner hosted by Trump for Chinese President Xi Jinping. The Huangs are seated at the top table alongside Trump, Xi and then-Apple CEO Tim Cook.

In October, the intelligence became public. The New York Times published a report detailing the 2025 intelligence briefings, putting these initial allegations into the public sphere.

November 2026, a second extramarital affair came to light following another New York Times article claiming Huang engaged in a relationship with Nvidia employee Kimberly Powell. Following a discussion with the board, Jensen Huang resigned as CEO.

Nvidia is the lynchpin of the current AI boom and demand for its chips has seen the company become one of the most valuable companies in the world. Today's news isn't going to change that but with investor confidence in AI expenditure starting to waver, we could see some long-term fallout further down the line.

"In the near-term, I think Nvidia will continue to perform as usual. The fundamentals won't change for CY 2027 and potentially CY 2028. A lot of these deals and supply chain are already locked up, Ryuta Makino, software and semiconductor analyst at Gabelli Funds, told Tom's Guide.

"The longer-term, post Feynman is where I would watch for. So 2029 and 2030 are years that may be impacted more broadly. There is potential that this will lower AI infrastructure spend in the long-term given that Nvidia will likely lose market share.

"This can also mean that lower efficiency gains on these servers equals lower AI efficiency and therefore the entire ecosystem will be worse overall. I am still assessing the impact but there will definitely be a ripple."

As U.S. markets open for the day, Nvidia's stock price is jumping up and down. I saw it open at 13% down before recovering somewhat to 8% down at the time of this writing but it's set to be a turbulent day for Wall Street.

So, who is the new Interim CEO of Nvidia? Colette Kress joined the company in September 2013 and is the executive vice president and chief financial officer. She has previously served nearly 25 years in a range of finance roles at major technology companies, including 13 years at Microsoft.

“Colette has helped lead NVIDIA through a period of extraordinary growth and has a deep understanding of our business, customers, operations and financial position,” said Harvey Jones, the newly-appointed chair of the Nvidia Board of Directors.

“She is supported by an experienced leadership team that has been instrumental in executing Nvidia’s strategy and advancing its technology roadmap. The Board has full confidence in Colette and the leadership team, and we expect the company’s operations, customer commitments and product roadmap to continue without interruption.”

The market isn't going to officially open until 9:30 am, but Nvidia shares have already fallen 10% in U.S. premarket trading after Huang's exit was announced.

Nvidia is one of the "Magnificent Seven" tech stocks, along with the likes of Apple, Amazon and Alphabet, that collectively make up over 30% of the S&P 500. A lot of standard 401(k) plans are heavily weighted in index funds that are tied to the performance of these companies. So today's news could have a knock-on effect for a lot of people.

In a press release announcing Huang's departure, Colette Kress, Interim CEO and CFO of Nvidia said: "I am committed to building on the extraordinary foundation Jensen created over the last 33 years.”

“We will continue advancing the work that has made Nvidia a leader in accelerated computing and AI, and execute on the opportunities ahead. Our focus remains on serving our customers, partners, developers and shareholders.”

The press release ended by saying the Nvidia Board and the company "thank Jensen for his immeasurable contributions to the company and the industry."

Nvidia has confirmed that, following Huang's departure, Colette Kress, current Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer will step into the role of Interim Chief Executive Officer.

"Kress will continue to serve as Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer while serving as Interim Chief Executive Officer until a permanent successor has been named," Nvidia said.

"The Board is initiating a search for a permanent Chief Executive Officer and will consider internal and external candidates."

Jensen Huang has announced his resignation as Nvidia's CEO.

Nvidia operates a famously flat structure with Jensen Huang actively involved in the company's routine operations. That said, one analyst told me his departure today is unlikely to torpedo the company's current AI focus.

"A prolonged leadership crisis could also disrupt product development or investment, but I think Jensen Huang's departure is unlikely to have any immediate effect on the price or availability of Nvidia products," said Louise Wooldridge, Senior Research Manager, Games, Ampere Analysis.

"There is also the possibility that, if Nvidia's competitive position is weakened by Huang leaving, other chipmakers (like AMD) could gain an advantage, and this stronger competition could improve the landscape for consumers.

"Overall, though, I think the commercial incentives pushing Nvidia towards AI will remain, regardless of the leadership situation, and so it is more likely that little will change in the long run."

This saga hit critical mass when The New York Times published a report detailing a long timeline of Huang’s alleged affair with Alice Huang, a suspected Chinese spy.

Following this report, Jensen admitted to an affair in an internal email to his staff, and while he didn’t outright admit it was with Alice Huang, the fact he spent part of his statement talking about “national security concerns,” and that he’s “proud and grateful to be an American,” seems to connect the dots.

I owe my family and all of you an apology.

I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.

Throughout my life, my family has given me love and support. They deserve my honesty and loyalty. Instead, I let them down and damaged the life we built together. I take full responsibility for what I did and the hurt I caused, and I accept the criticism that comes with it.

To my wife and family: I love you. I know an apology cannot undo what I have done. I hope our family will heal and that, over time, I can earn back your trust.

To my colleagues at NVIDIA, including those I have worked alongside for decades, and to our board, partners, and shareholders around the world: you deserve better from me. Leading NVIDIA is the privilege of my life. My responsibility is to serve you and be worthy of your trust. I have fallen short of that responsibility. I am fully committed to NVIDIA and will work to earn back your confidence.

Regarding the national security concerns raised in news reports, NVIDIA’s Board of Directors has initiated an independent investigation. I support the investigation and will cooperate fully. I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting NVIDIA and supporting America’s national security. I am proud and grateful to be an American.

Quite possibly. According to an exclusive report from the Wall Street Journal, Nvidia's board "is preparing to oust CEO Jensen Huang" and that it would leave "one of the world’s most valuable companies in need of a new leader."

However, there's no immediate successor who could replace the leather jacket-wearing CEO who has become the face of the current AI arms race.

Dan Ives, a tech analyst at Wedbush Securities described Huang as the "central nervous system" of the U.S. technology ecosystem. Ives went as far as calling him "irreplaceable" and warned that losing him would disrupt not just Nvidia, but the broader tech ecosystem. According to Ives, should Huang leave Nvidia, his immediate exit could trigger a 25%–30% stock drop.

Nvidia's board has 11 members, including Huang, that are meeting today to consider whether to dismiss Jensen from his position following an internal investigation launched on November 8.

The ten other board members are independent and have the power to fire the CEO on the grounds of breaking the company's ethical standards. We are expecting a result to be announced later today on the verdict they've reached — even if that verdict is a further delay.

#3180. Apple TV 4K review: The best streamer comes at a cost

It’s been four years since Apple last updated the Apple TV 4K, but a new version is here. There’s Siri AI support, a faster chip, an improved remote, and more.

Here’s everything that’s changed, what’s better, and whether the new Apple TV 4K justifies its new $299 price.

The Apple TV 4K’s overall design is largely unchanged. It’s still the same familiar black box that sits underneath your television. The only visual change is that the front status light has moved from the right side to the center.

Inside, Apple has upgraded the A15 Bionic to the A19 chip, touting 50% faster CPU performance and twice the GPU performance.

Those are great improvements on paper. In practice, I’m not doing anything on my Apple TV that really stresses the performance. Compared to my third-generation Apple TV 4K, I’ve occasionally noticed slightly smoother animations and faster performance in apps that handle more processing locally, like Infuse.

I think the biggest advantage of the A19 chip is future-proofing. People tend to buy and keep these devices for years. In fact, I’m still using a first-generation Apple TV 4K from 2017 in my bedroom, and it still works just fine nearly a decade later. The A19 gives the new Apple TV plenty of performance headroom for future tvOS updates and more demanding apps, even if those advantages aren’t particularly noticeable today.

The Siri Remote looks the same as before, but it now supports Precision Finding in the Find My app, making it easier to track down when misplaced. You can also play a sound on the remote to help locate it. I lose my Siri Remote all the time, so this honestly might be the change I’ve noticed and appreciated most in my 10 days testing the new Apple TV.

It’s worth noting Apple also sells the new Siri Remote separately for $59, and it’s compatible with every previous Apple TV 4K generation. You do, however, need a newer iPhone model to use Precision Finding.

One of the more interesting new features is support for a four-HomePod surround sound system. You need four HomePod (2nd generation) or HomePod mini 2 speakers, arranged in matching pairs at the front and rear of the room. Apple TV automatically calibrates the speakers based on their positions in the room.

For context, I typically use my Apple TV with a stereo pair of full-size HomePod (2nd generation) speakers. I’ve spent some time testing the new four-speaker surround sound setup by adding a pair of HomePod mini 2 speakers.

My house’s layout isn’t particularly well-suited for a traditional surround sound setup, but to my admittedly untrained ears, this sounds great. I can’t speak to how it compares to a dedicated surround sound system, but I appreciate Apple continuing to expand what’s possible with HomePods and Apple TV.

One of the biggest changes with the new Apple TV 4K is the addition of three far-field microphones. This means you can now interact with Siri without picking up the Siri Remote. In conjunction with this, Siri AI is also coming to Apple TV.

Siri AI brings the same broad world knowledge and personal-context capabilities you’ve experienced on iPhone and HomeView, but adapts them to finding and watching content on your television. Siri AI on Apple TV requires the owner of your Apple Home setup to have an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone or iPad.

Personal context requests also require a paired compatible device connected to the same Wi-Fi network as Apple TV.

What was that TV show Lily recommended a few weeks ago?

What are some baseball movies I might like?

What did the vet say after Blake’s vet appointment?

For each example, tvOS responded with a dedicated interface on Apple TV, showing the answer along with poster art, cast information, and more. It also offers built-in contextual suggestions when you ask for recommendations, so you can refine the results further.

You can also ask Siri contextual questions about the show or movie you’re watching. This includes things like “where was this show filmed?” and “when is the next season coming out?”

I’ve found Siri AI’s responses to those contextual questions less accurate. It struggles to accurately identify the show or movie that’s playing, leading to completely inaccurate responses to those types of questions.

It’s worth noting that Siri AI is also coming to the second-generation Apple TV 4K from 2021 and the third-generation model from 2022. The far-field microphones are what’s exclusive to the new hardware. This lets you shout Siri commands into the air without talking directly into the Siri Remote.

In my testing, hands-free Siri works relatively well, and it’s convenient to control Apple TV without reaching for the remote. It does a good job at picking up commands

I can’t go any further in this review without talking about the price. The Apple TV 4K (4th generation) costs $299. That’s a huge increase over previous Apple TV models. Here’s a brief history of Apple TV 4K pricing over the years to set the stage:

After Apple introduced the $129 Apple TV model in October 2022, I started to notice a change. More and more people had Apple TVs when I would visit. Friends and family who had previously bought an Amazon or Roku box, or just used their TV’s built-in software, had purchased an Apple TV.

At $299, I worry that type of adoption is going to come to a screeching halt. And it’s unfortunate because the Apple TV is so much better than anything else out there. tvOS is fast, clean, and relatively free of the clutter and advertisements you find on competing platforms. The Siri Remote is excellent, and the integration with the rest of Apple’s ecosystem is hard to beat.

I could justify the $299 price for the Apple TV 4K (4th generation) if it were just one option available in a broader lineup. If there were lower-priced options for people who don’t need all the bells and whistles. That’s not the case, though. In fact, this is the first Apple TV 4K generation to be sold in just one configuration. There’s no cheaper version with less storage or fewer features.

To Apple’s credit, these are devices that can last for years. The fact that I’m still using an Apple TV 4K from 2017 makes the $299 price a tiny bit easier to swallow, but it doesn’t really change my frustration.

Apple seems serious about its new smart home strategy. There’s the HomeView smart display, a new HomePod mini, and the Apple Home Collection family of smart home accessories launching later this year. One of the best ways to get deeper into people’s homes is by controlling how they watch TV. I can’t help but think pricing the Apple TV 4K out of reach for so many people will hinder those ambitions.

Don’t get me wrong, I love the Apple TV. I have three of them in my house. If one of them broke, I would reluctantly pay $299 for a new one. Whether you fall into that category is for you to decide. All I can say is that the new Apple TV 4K is the best streamer on the market.

#3179. 2 Quantum Computing Stocks That Could Help Set You Up for Life

IBM and Quantinuum are publicly arguing about how quantum computing will be won, and I think a lifetime investor should own both sides of that argument.

Last week, the two quantum companies I'd most want to own for 20 years made opposite cases for how to win this sector of the economy. On Nov. 5, Quantinuum (QNT -4.35%) raised its 2026 revenue outlook and touted an accuracy record on its Helios computer. A day later, IBM (IBM -0.86%) switched on its most advanced quantum computer in Chicago, powered by its Nighthawk chip.

Here's quantum computing in brief. Regular computers use bits that are either 0 or 1. Quantum computers use qubits, which can hold a blend of both and link together, letting them tackle problems like simulating molecules that overwhelm ordinary chips. But qubits are fragile and error-prone, so the race is to bundle many of them into one reliable "logical qubit." The usual question is which quantum stock has the most upside. I think the better one is which side of the industry's biggest argument you want to own. My answer is both.

There's also a referee now. In September, the Department of Energy launched a competition (with funding still unapproved) that pays companies from a $100 million prize pool to demonstrate a quantum computer with at least 100 logical qubits, with a 2028 goal.

On its third-quarter call, IBM said its latest Nighthawk chip runs 100,000 circuits per second, then claimed a workload costing about $100 on IBM could cost up to $10 million on "slower competitive modalities." That reads like a shot at trapped-ion machines such as Quantinuum's. It also reached Stage C of DARPA's Quantum Benchmarking Initiative and signed 16 enterprise quantum engagements this year, including one with General Motors (GM -0.38%).

The move I like most came Nov. 5, when IBM launched an error-correction platform with Advanced Micro Devices (AMD +1.58%) and Oak Ridge National Laboratory, pairing its quantum machines with an AMD-powered supercomputer. IBM's Starling system, planned for 2029, is designed to run 100 million operations on 200 logical qubits.

IBM is the lower-stress way to own quantum because it pays you to wait. At about $246 per share, it pays a dividend that yields roughly 2.7%, and the company produced $7.8 billion in free cash flow through nine months of 2026. At its Dec. 10 Quantum Day, I want the company to provide a fresh dollar figure on quantum contracts above the $1.1 billion it has signed since 2017.

Quantinuum's pitch is the opposite: be right first, get fast later. In October, Helios reached 99.9995% logical fidelity, an error rate the company says is 100 times lower than the best published result on any other hardware. Its next machine, Sol, is on track for the second half of 2027 and will be tuned toward 100 logical qubits. If it hits that mark (a big "if"), it would clear the DOE's bar a year early.

The overlooked piece is software. On Nov. 5, Quantinuum laid out a roadmap for its Nexus developer platform, designed so customers' code carries forward to each new machine through its 2029 Apollo system. Nexus now supports more than 200 organizations, up 45% this year.

I picked Quantinuum over IonQ (IONQ -4.08%), the bigger revenue story, because nearly half of IonQ's third-quarter sales came from the SkyWater chip foundry it bought, not quantum computing.

This is the pricier half. At about $40, the stock sits a third below its June IPO price of $60, yet the whole company is worth roughly $10.6 billion against 2026 revenue guidance of $31 million to $34 million.

The number I'll watch is Sol's logical error rate. Quantinuum is targeting 1 error per 100,000 operations at 100 logical qubits in late 2027.Hit it on time, and I'd keep adding. Slip into 2028, and that premium gets hard to defend.

I'd make IBM the core holding and keep Quantinuum smaller, sized for a tech stock that has ranged from $28 to $87 since its June IPO. One of these companies is trying to finish the race first. The other is trying to finish it without a mistake. For a lifetime holding, I don't need to know which one physics favors. I just need to own both.

#3178. The Dynamo-Electric Principle: 160 Years of Powering Industry

How a breakthrough in electromechanical energy conversion helped shape the motors and generators that drive modern industry

Innomotics is a global leader in electric motors and large drive systems, operating from its headquarters in Nuremberg, Germany.

The dynamo-electric principle: one idea, 160 years, millions of motors.

This article is brought to you by Innomotics.

In the annals of industrial history, few innovations have demonstrated such remarkable staying power as the dynamo-electric principle. Discovered by Werner von Siemens in 1866, this groundbreaking principle remains fundamental to modern electrical engineering more than a century and a half later – and continues to shape the technology portfolio of Innomotics, a globally leading provider of electric motors and large drive systems. What began as a breakthrough in electromechanical energy conversion has evolved into a cornerstone of global industry – powering everything from brewery operations in Qingdao to high-voltage drive systems in petrochemical plants.

The year 1866 marked a decisive turning point, not only in the broader arc of industrial transformation but specifically in the realm of electric motion. At a time when Europe was entering a new phase of industrial transformation, Werner von Siemens pioneered the dynamo-electric principle – a breakthrough that enabled electric machines to generate their own magnetic field through self-excitation. This innovation transformed electric machines from laboratory curiosities into practical power sources, enabling the widespread electrification of industry and infrastructure that defined the late 19th century.

This electric motor from Innomotics was installed in the early 1900s at the historic Tsingtao Brewery in China and supported production processes for more than 90 years, operating continuously under industrial conditions.Innomotics

The principle itself is elegantly simple: an iron core generates a stable magnetic field; a rotating coil is placed within this field; movement in the magnetic field induces an electric current; part of this current strengthens the magnetic field; and electrical energy is continuously converted into motion. This self-reinforcing cycle made efficient and reliable electric motion possible – and it remains the foundation of modern motors today.

More than 160 years later, the same fundamental idea continues to power industrial applications around the world. Millions of motors operate reliably under demanding conditions, keeping production running across generations. The dynamo-electric principle made it possible for electric machines to convert electrical energy into motion (and motion back into electrical energy), creating the technological foundation for modern electric motors and drive systems.

Active Vibration Control System (AVCS) enhances stability and reliability by actively reducing vibrations.Innomotics

Perhaps no example illustrates this longevity better than the electric motor from Innomotics at the historic Tsingtao Brewery in China. Installed in the early 1900s during the early electrification of industrial brewing, this motor supported production processes for more than 90 years, operating continuously under industrial conditions. It became a powerful example of long-term reliability in real-world applications – a testament to how engineering ensures reliable motion across decades.

Continuity, however, does not mean stagnation. Sixteen decades after the original breakthrough, innovations continue to emerge that build upon this proven foundation. Two recent developments – the Active Vibration Control System (AVCS) and oil-lubricated rolling bearings (OLRB) – carry this spirit of innovation and ingenuity forward, a commitment that has been recognized with the German Innovation Award.

Innomotics’ patented Oil-Lubricated Rolling Bearing (OLRB) technology enhances reliability and reduces maintenance requirements.Innomotics

AVCS helps optimize high-voltage motor performance by actively decoupling motors from their foundations to reduce vibration issues. OLRB helps prevent rolling bearing failures from the start with continuous lubrication, supporting higher availability, less downtime, and long-term cost savings. These innovations demonstrate how the basic principle of 1866 can be enhanced through modern engineering to meet contemporary demands for reliability and efficiency.

For three decades, with over 25,000 units driving performance globally, Innomotics’ Perfect Harmony GH180 medium-voltage drive platform has supported reliable operation across industries. Its modular architecture enables efficient power control, high availability, and long-term performance. With thousands of installations worldwide, Perfect Harmony GH180 continues to build on a proven technological foundation, minimizing downtime and ensuring stable production.

Keeping critical motors running requires the right expertise and innovation spirit throughout the entire lifecycle. With Innomotics Customer Services, operators and plant managers gain the insights they need to maintain reliability and optimize maintenance strategies. Winding Lifetime Analysis (WLA) combines operating history, machine measurements, and physics-based modeling to assess the condition of the winding insulation and estimate its remaining useful lifetime. This enables informed maintenance decisions, reduces uncertainty, and helps minimize the risk of unplanned downtime.

The Perfect Harmony GH180 delivers efficient, reliable and flexible medium-voltage drive performance.Innomotics

What began as a breakthrough in 1866 still brings its value to modern industry. The dynamo-electric principle made efficient and reliable electric motion possible – and it remains the foundation of modern motors today.

As industries worldwide grapple with challenges ranging from energy efficiency to operational resilience, this 160-year-old principle continues to prove its relevance.

For plant managers and engineers seeking long-term performance in demanding applications, the message is clear: the foundation laid in the 19th century remains as solid as ever. What has changed are the tools and services built upon it – from vibration control systems to predictive analytics – all designed to extract maximum value from a principle that has, quite literally, powered the modern world for a century and a half.

Innomotics, carrying forward a legacy that spans the full arc of this history, continues to move industry forward with innovations that create real progress. The dynamo-electric principle may be 160 years old, but as the company’s portfolio demonstrates, it is far from obsolete. It is, in every sense of the word, still running.
