#3177. Apple HomeView review: An adorable smart display that earns its place

Apple’s HomeView smart display is here. It combines a 7-inch display with Siri AI and an all-new software experience that actually feels really familiar.

I’ve spent the last ten days living with HomeView in my kitchen. Here’s everything you need to know.

HomeView is an adorable little thing. That’s the best way to describe it. A 7-inch square display sits atop a rounded aluminum speaker base. A small, polished metal arm connects it and lets you tilt the display forward and backward.

HomeView comes in four colors: Starlight, Rose Pink, Silver, and Space Gray. My review unit is Starlight, and it’s very subtle. I had to double-check the box to make sure it was Starlight, not Silver.

The decision to make the display square is interesting. Between that design and the software experience centered around faces and widgets, HomeView really does feel like an oversized Apple Watch for your home.

I really appreciate the square display. It makes HomeView look less like an iPad propped up on a stand and more like a dedicated, purpose-driven device.

In terms of specs, the 7-inch display has a 1088 × 1088 resolution, equating to a pixel density of 220 pixels per inch. Max brightness is 500 nits. It can also dim all the way to 0.3 nits, which means it can go in a bedroom without being a nuisance. It also has True Tone to match your room’s lighting temperature.

For the past ten days, my partner and I have been living with HomeView on our kitchen counter. The square display and aluminum base look great in that setting. I don’t think an iPad-style display would look nearly as intentional. We also don’t have much spare counter space. If HomeView were any bigger or wider, I’m not sure we’d have room for it.

In the lead-up to HomeView’s launch, I was skeptical of how usable a 7-inch display would be. In practice, I’ve found this to be (mostly) a non-issue. Apple has done a great job optimizing the interface for the display. Text is readable at a glance from a few feet away, timers are nice and large, and the interface adapts to show more information when you’re closer.

Sometimes I wish it were bigger. Viewing a recipe requires a bit more scrolling than I would like. It’d be nice to fit a couple more widgets on the Modular face. But those trade-offs are easier to accept when I consider how much I appreciate HomeView’s compact footprint.

Apple touts that the HomeView has a custom-engineered acoustic system. There are two custom full-range drivers in the display, paired with a down-firing woofer and two force-canceling passive radiators in the base.

In practice, HomeView’s sound quality falls somewhere between the HomePod mini and the full-size second-generation HomePod. Its sound quality won’t blow you away, but it’s respectable for music and podcast playback. I replaced a full-size original HomePod in my kitchen with it, and while it doesn’t sound quite as good, it makes up for it in other ways … like by having a screen.

HomeView can serve as an AirPlay target, too, so you can beam content from your iPhone or other Apple device right to it. You can also AirPlay from HomeView to other AirPlay targets in your house.

HomeView doesn’t have any buttons, which is a design decision I’ve found very frustrating on multiple occasions. I wish it had volume buttons, so I could quickly adjust the volume without yelling at Siri or using the touchscreen.

HomeView’s software borrows heavily from iOS and watchOS. The interface is built around a system of faces with widgets, very similar to the Apple Watch’s complications system. The process of configuring a face will feel very familiar to Apple Watch and iPhone users.

You can customize faces by long-pressing on them, which reveals a familiar “Customize” screen. Here, you can change the style, color, widgets, and background. You can also add widgets from your nearby iPhone. Apple says that widgets are visible to everyone, but widget content is only visible while your primary device is in the home.

I’ve become particularly fond of the Modular face, which lets you place four equally sized square widgets. I think it provides a nice amount of glanceable information without feeling too dense. The Photos face is also a delight, essentially turning the HomeView into a digital picture frame. Support for Shared Albums is especially nice.

I think Apple made the right decision by building the HomeView experience around faces rather than a traditional app-focused interface. Most of the time, HomeView is just sitting on your counter or table, and you’re not actively interacting with it. That’s why I’ve gravitated towards the Modular face.

The faces system also means that HomeView doesn’t constantly demand your attention. Just like the physical design, it’s there when you need it, but otherwise does a good job blending into the background.

Swiping down from the left two-thirds of the display activates Siri AI, while swiping down from the top right takes you to Control Center. Swiping up from the bottom takes you to the Home Screen, where you’ll find a grid of apps and spots to add even more widgets.

There is no App Store on HomeView. Instead, there’s a collection of built-in Apple apps paired with audio and video apps through its CarPlay-based app system. Here are the Apple apps that are available on HomeView:

I’m hopeful that Apple builds on the app story for HomeView sooner rather than later. I don’t think HomeView needs its own App Store, but I do think it needs more apps. This includes more Apple apps and additional third-party apps.

I desperately want Apple to add the Notes app to HomeView. My wife and I keep recipes and dinner ideas in Notes, so it would be great to have that experience available on HomeView. It feels like an odd omission right now.

I think the idea of basing the system on CarPlay makes sense. There are a lot of similarities in UI between how an app should work in the car and on a smart display. The Audible app, for example, translates really well from CarPlay to HomeView, as does Spotify.

However, the list of supported categories for CarPlay is a lot broader than the audio and video category Apple is allowing on HomeView right now. There are signs this could expand very soon, and I’m hopeful that’s the case.

One of the cleverest aspects of HomeView is its recipe experience. When you open a recipe in Safari, HomeView gives you the option to convert it into a dedicated cooking interface. You can browse for recipes directly on HomeView, or find one on your iPhone and simply hold it in front of HomeView to hand off the webpage.

HomeView then intelligently detects the actual recipe information and puts it into a streamlined interface. You can view the full ingredient list and measurements, and check off items as you go. The recipe itself is broken down into individual steps. It also intelligently identifies when you need to set a timer and gives you the option to start one directly from the recipe.

This is the exact type of feature that’s perfect for HomeView, and perfect for a dedicated screen sitting on the kitchen counter. You don’t have to keep reaching for your phone, unlocking it, and finding your place in the recipe.

The feature works incredibly well. I tried it with recipes of varying lengths from multiple different websites without any major problems.

There are some limitations, though. For example, it does struggle if a website splits the recipe into multiple pages. Also, as I mentioned earlier, the 7-inch display means there’s more scrolling involved than I’d like. It doesn’t solve my frustration with the lack of a dedicated Notes app. Still, it’s a great example of where this design excels.

Ultimately, the HomeView’s software interface is really well done. Delightful animations appear throughout the experience, like when notifications or the Siri blob slide in from the top bezel. Everything feels very smooth. The software feels familiar because of its similarities to Apple Watch and iPhone, but it’s also clearly purpose-built for the smart display form factor.

Since HomeView is meant for everyone in your home, Apple had to engineer a multi-user system. HomeView supports up to six people, each with their own personalized Home Screen, widgets, and access to personal information.

HomeView identifies the different people in your house in two ways: facial recognition and voice recognition. The goal is to recognize who’s interacting with it and customize the experience for that person. So, when I approach HomeView, it can recognize my face and display my calendar, reminders, and messages. When my wife approaches, it can recognize her instead and show her information.

The facial recognition implementation is particularly interesting. HomeView doesn’t have Face ID. Instead, it uses its built-in camera for facial recognition. During setup, you’re asked to turn your head left, right, up, and down so HomeView can capture your face from different angles.

In practice, HomeView’s facial recognition works surprisingly well. I was skeptical, but it’s done a good job of identifying both my wife and me. If I approach it and try to open the Messages app while it’s on my wife’s profile, I get a message saying it can’t verify my identity. If I repeatedly try, HomeView disables facial recognition, requiring my wife to authenticate using her iPhone before she can access her personal information again.

In addition to protecting personal data, HomeView does a decent job of automatically switching between profiles. There’s occasionally a delay of a few seconds, so I wish it were slightly faster.

HomeView is powered by Apple’s A18 chip, which enables support for Siri AI. However, Siri AI works a bit differently on HomeView than on other Apple devices.

HomeView can answer world knowledge questions on its own, without relying on a paired iPhone or iPad. This is basically the trivia questions we’ve all grown accustomed to shouting at voice assistants over the years. The difference, of course, is that Siri AI answers these questions well, unlike old Siri. On HomeView, the experience is even better because you can visually see the response on the display, often accompanied by images or other visual information.

The second aspect of Siri AI is personal context. To use Siri AI’s personal context on HomeView, you need an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone or iPad in your house.

Apple says that the device must have been recently unlocked and be connected to the same Wi-Fi network as HomeView.

In my testing over the last 10 days, I’ve never run into a situation where HomeView was unable to answer a Siri AI query because my iPhone was unavailable.

I’ve found Siri AI to be quite impressive and useful since it debuted in September. It’s a huge upgrade over old Siri. Broadly speaking, that experience extends to HomeView.

Many of the same personal context questions I ask on my iPhone can now be answered by HomeView. And because of HomeView’s form factor, it’s more useful when multitasking. Instead of reaching for my iPhone or hoping it’s within earshot, I can just ask HomeView.

Here are a few questions HomeView has answered without a hiccup:

In terms of speed, I’ve found HomeView to be slightly slower to answer personal context questions than my iPhone Duo. It’s not a huge difference, but it’s a few seconds each time. I assume this is because HomeView is basically handing off the request to my iPhone, adding an additional step that requests directly on the iPhone don’t have to do.

Siri AI is not without its faults. There are times on HomeView where it just hangs and never responds, or responds with a generic “Sorry, try again later” message of some sort. HomeView’s primary interaction method is your voice, which makes these types of Siri AI failures even more frustrating.

HomeView can also serve as the command center for your smart home. It has a dedicated Home app, as well as multiple different Home-focused face options. You can also, of course, use your voice to control HomeKit accessories and scenes through Siri.

There’s ultimately nothing particularly remarkable about HomeView’s support for smart home control. It offers much of the same functionality as the Home app on your iPhone, but in one central location that everyone in your house can use.

There is one limitation: you currently can’t use Siri AI on HomeView to control secure devices like locks and garage doors, even if the device recognizes you. If they are part of a scene, you can tell Siri AI to set the scene and it works. But you can’t individually control them.

Apple tells Joanna Stern that a software update coming next month will add security accessory support to HomeView’s Siri AI.

I wish Apple would expand what HomeView can do for the smart home. It has a built-in camera, so why can’t I use that camera for motion sensing or as a HomeKit Secure Video camera?

I’ve found the screen most useful for quickly checking the status of accessories, like seeing whether a door is locked or glancing at the doorbell camera. For actually controlling accessories, I still find Siri and automations to be the easiest approach. HomeView hasn’t really changed that, although I do appreciate being able to adjust the thermostat right from the kitchen counter.

HomeView costs $299, which is about $100 less than I expected based on rumors. That’s a surprisingly reasonable price, I think. The key, of course, is whether you’ll actually use it day to day.

When you get a new iPhone, you already have a pretty good idea of what you’ll use it for and where it fits into your life. New features might change how you use it, but the core functionality stays the same.

HomeView is very different. At first, it sits on your counter and is nice to look at. It’s a very, very cute little thing. But it takes time to discover how and why it fits into your life.

At first, I had no idea whether I’d actually use HomeView. But in the ten days it’s been sitting on my counter, it’s grown on me quite a bit. It’s gone from being a nice-to-have to something I use and rely on for multiple tasks each day.

It’s also been interesting watching my partner interact with it. Her first impression was essentially, “It’s cute, but I don’t know what I’ll use it for.” Over the last week, however, she’s remarked multiple times how much she likes it.

Whether it’s personal context-focused Siri AI interactions, simply being able to glance and see how long is left on a timer, watching the animated album art as a song plays, or the joy of the Photos face, HomeView has earned its spot.

In fact, I moved HomeView from our kitchen to my office for a day to test a few features and settings in more depth. While cooking dinner that night, we both found ourselves shouting Siri commands into the air and glancing at the empty spot on the counter, only to remember it wasn’t there.

I think that’s the best illustration of what makes HomeView special. You don’t have to be a HomeKit enthusiast or spend hours tinkering with smart home automations to appreciate it. It’s a device everyone in the house can find their own uses for, and it becomes more useful the longer it’s part of your routine.

Google and Samsung's "intelligent eyewear" AI glasses are finally launching today (Nov. 12) with designs from Gentle Monster and Warby Parker. The Meta Ray-Ban rivals utilize Google's Gemini AI platform to bring "real-time assistance" throughout your day.

Starting at $395, intelligent eyewear costs much less than the Ray-Ban Meta (gen 3) glasses, but Meta still sells the Gen 1 and Gen 2 versions, plus a variety of styles with varying prices.

Read on to see what Google and Samsung are offering and how to pre-order a pair.

Google and Samsung partnered with Gentle Monster and Warby Parker to produce frames that are meant to look more stylish and like a normal pair of glasses.

Gentle Monster's collection includes six designs in multiple colors, including pink, dark red, gray and yellow, which can be paired with tinted, clear, blue or brown lenses. The Gentle Monster frames are more premium, with a starting price of $449.

Warby Parker's designs come in three styles — Alden, Reid and Wren — which are inspired by existing Warby Parker frames. You can choose optical or sun styles in "Pine, Saddles or Jet Black" colorways.

Prescription lenses are available for both Gentle Monster and Warby Parker options.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Google says that the frames weigh around 41 grams. For comparison, the Ray-Ban Meta Wayfarer design weighs 51.5 grams and the newer Aviators weigh 54.5 grams.

The glasses feature open ear speakers that can provide the Gemini voice as well as music from YouTube or audiobooks.

They do feature a 12MP ultra-wide camera for capturing photos and videos by pressing a button or asking Gemini.

Meta has faced increasing backlash over what have been deemed "pervert glasses," including increased scrutiny from international governments.

According to Google, camera visuals are not saved in your Gemini history or used for AI training or ad targeting. The company says that your data is encrypted even if it leaves the glasses for processing on your phone or in the cloud.

You have control over what apps can access the camera, as they need to ask permission, which you can revoke. Gemini history can be reviewed and deleted as needed. Though, one aspect is that you may need to go into settings and tell Gemini if your chats can be used in generative AI models.

Like Meta's glasses, an LED light turns on to indicate when the camera is recording. Similarly, the light is designed to detect tampering and prevent photos or videos.

Google claims the glasses are designed to redact faces before sending images to Gemini.

Google is bringing its Gemini AI platform to intelligent eyewear glasses. It's similar to how you would expect AI to work on smart glasses.

You can access Google apps and services hands-free by saying "Hey Gemini" or tapping the frames to ask for recommendations or learn about what the cameras can see. Examples provided by Google include adding items to your grocery list or checking your Uber status while keeping your eyes up.

During Google I/O back in May, we didn't get a chance to test out the official intelligent eyewear glasses. Google only had prototypes available, but we did try the software.

"Gemini Live is the key to making these true Ray-Ban Meta beaters, and it frankly makes Meta AI seem feeble in comparison," my colleague Jason England said at the time. "Rather than having to follow rudimentary vocal steps to do certain things, a press and hold on the stem turns it on and I’m having a full conversational interaction with the AI about the world around me."

He was able to get turn-by-turn directions using Google Maps and AI image generation using Nano Banana.

Pre-orders are now open on both the Gentle Monster and Warby Parker websites and in their retail stores. You can also pre-order directly from Google here.

If you want to wait, Intelligent eyewear will hit store shelves on December 10, where you can purchase both in-person and online.

The glasses work with Pixel and Samsung phones and even Apple's iPhones.

#3175. Top Wall Street analysts are confident about these 3 stocks for the long haul

Global stock markets have been under pressure as geopolitical tensions have resurfaced in the Middle East. Moreover, investors remain concerned about the sustainability of AI-driven demand and infrastructure spending.

Nonetheless, those looking for attractive stock picks amid the ongoing volatility can gain key insights by tracking the recommendations of top Wall Street analysts. These experts assign ratings after in-depth analysis of a company's fundamentals, growth opportunities, and risks.

Here are three stocks favored by some of Wall Street's top pros, according to TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

E-commerce and cloud computing giant Amazon (AMZN) is this week's first pick. Heading into the company's second-quarter earnings, TD Cowen analyst John Blackledge reiterated a buy rating on AMZN stock, citing strength in the Amazon Web Services cloud unit as well as the e-commerce and advertising businesses. The analyst lowered his price target on AMZN stock to $340 from $350 as he revised his estimates and slightly raised his capex projections.

Specifically, Blackledge expects Amazon to report revenue of $200.1 billion, 2% above the Street's consensus, driven by acceleration in AWS and advertising revenue. He also expects the company's e-commerce business to reflect the shifting of Prime Day in the U.S. and other key markets to the second quarter this year, compared with third quarter of last year.

In particular, Blackledge expects AWS revenue to grow 35.5% year-over-year in Q2 2026, marking an acceleration from 28.4% in the prior-year quarter and 3.4% above the Street's expectations. The 5-star analyst expects revenue to be driven by rising generative AI workloads as the company's significant AI infrastructure spending helps to ease supply constraints.

Regarding third-quarter outlook, Blackledge said, "Our rev and Op Income estimates are 0.3% and 3.2% above consensus, driven by further AWS revenue growth acceleration led by AI demand."

Blackledge ranks No. 771 among more than 12,300 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 55% of the time, delivering an average return of 11.2%. See Amazon Ownership Structure on TipRanks.

Moving on to semiconductor company Marvell Technology (MRVL). Following several meetings with management, RBC Capital analyst Srini Pajjuri reiterated a buy rating on MRVL stock with a price target of $360.

"Overall, the meetings reinforced our conviction that MRVL can sustain 40%+ growth for the next 3 years, driven by strong AI demand, optical connectivity leadership, and expanding Custom pipeline," said Pajjuri.

The 5-star analyst added that robust demand and limited supply are giving greater revenue visibility. Pajjuri noted that Marvell's data center business is on track to deliver more than 50% growth this year and next. Also, the growth in the company's networking business is outpacing compute, driven by agentic AI and inferencing workloads.

Meanwhile, Pajjuri noted that optical product lead times have extended to more than six months, while XPU customers are placing purchase orders 12 months in advance. While the analyst kept his estimates unchanged, he sees the possibility of upside for the second half of 2026 from the Optical business, with more significant upside potential for 2027 and 2028 estimates.

Furthermore, Pajjuri noted that Marvell's scale-across offering is emerging as an additional growth catalyst for 2027, while scale-up networking is expected to present a multibillion-dollar greenfield serviceable addressable market. Also, management is upbeat about Marvell's custom business, with the company targeting more than $10 billion in revenue for 2028, driven by existing programs with Amazon's AWS and Microsoft and multiple XPU attach wins.

#3174. 2 Years Until the Next Election. What Long-Term Investors Should Do With the Next 24 Months.

Don't let elections make you overreact with your investment decisions.

The 2026 midterm elections delivered a sweeping victory for the Democratic Party and a rebuke to President Donald Trump. Well-known red states like Texas turned mostly blue. Democrats will soon control the U.S. House and Senate by strong margins.

Depending on how you voted last week, you might be feeling the thrill of victory or the disappointment of defeat. But try not to let your political views affect how you invest. Even if your chosen candidates fall short at the polls, long-term investors are usually better off ignoring elections and focusing on fundamentals like economic growth, inflation, and corporate earnings.

Let's look at why elections don't matter much for your investments, and how to use the next 24 months before the 2028 elections to set up your portfolio for long-term success.

It's not correct to say that "elections don't matter." The parties in power have a massive impact on public policy. Decisions in state capitals and Washington, D.C., affect the everyday lives of hundreds of millions of Americans and countless others around the world.

The election of different politicians and parties can also be good or bad news for specific companies or industries. Different parties in power can enact new taxes or regulations that harm some companies, or create new incentives or government spending plans that benefit others.

For example, the recent midterm election showed a wide bipartisan backlash against artificial intelligence (AI) data centers. If a politician gets elected promising to limit or slow down the construction of AI data centers and follows through on that pledge, that could be bad news for semiconductor stocks or other AI-related stocks.

But in the long run, U.S. politicians from both parties don't tend to hurt stock market growth. 2024 research from U.S. Bancorp found that, in the medium- to long-term, elections have "minimal impact" on financial market performance. The bank's analysis also found that economic and inflation trends have a larger impact than election results on market returns.

Politicians have a lot of power, but they don't control the U.S. economy. Over the long run, American businesses tend to get better at solving problems, creating must-have products, and delivering strong earnings for shareholders. The S&P 500 (^GSPC -0.43%) goes up most of the time, regardless of who's in power in government.

Over the past 98 years, since 1928, the S&P 500 has delivered positive one-year returns in 72 of those years. That means you have about a 67% chance of earning a positive return from buying and holding an S&P 500 ETF for one year.

If you hold your stocks even longer, the chances get better. According to S&P 500 historical returns data compiled by Capital Group , holding the S&P 500 for three years delivers a positive return 88% of the time. A five-year holding period delivers positive returns 93% of the time. And 10-year periods deliver positive returns close to 100% of the time.

There's no 100% guaranteed "sure thing" in investing. But simply buying and holding the S&P 500 tends to deliver.

For example, the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF (VOO -0.58%) has delivered strong returns for long-term investors. VOO has delivered annualized returns of about 14.9% in the past 16 years, 15.5% in the past 10 years, and 12% in the past five years.

How should you invest for the next two years? For most people, the answer is to just keep buying stocks according to your long-term plan. Don't make any drastic moves based on short-term fears and doubts or try to predict the future.

Even if you have strong convictions about what the latest election is going to do for specific companies or sectors, the rest of the market might have already priced in those outcomes. For example, if you believe the Democrats' big win will be bad for AI data centers and semiconductor stocks ... millions of other investors might believe that too, and they might have already made that trade. The market can move faster than you.

If you're seriously losing sleep or suffering anxiety about your stocks, you might want to make a few changes in your portfolio. You might want to consider diversifying or de-risking by adding more bonds to your investment mix.

But if you're really in this for the long term, two years isn't a big deal. Keep buying a diversified portfolio of stocks. Hold on to them for at least five years. Let the economy do its work for you.

When our analyst team has a stock tip, it can pay to listen. After all, Stock Advisor's total average return is 835%* — a market-crushing outperformance compared to 208% for the S&P 500.

They just revealed what they believe are the 10 best stocks for investors to buy right now, available when you join Stock Advisor.

#3173. Google’s new Android XR glasses work with iOS, Made for iPhone certified

Google today announced Android XR audio glasses called Intelligent Eyewear that notably support iOS with Made for iPhone certification.

Hands-on: Google and Samsung’s vision for Android XR glasses is 20/20

Intelligent Eyewear is made by Samsung with frame designs from Gentle Monster and Warby Parker. There are 30 unique designs in total, and the frames weigh 40-44 grams with a 12-megapixel ultra-wide camera.

Google’s Glasses companion client for iOS handles compute, including HDR processing, and saves images and videos (up to 90 seconds) to Apple Photos. The Made for iPhone certification comes into play for Wi-Fi Aware connectivity that allows for fast media transfers.

Gemini commands that use the camera, like visual search or translation, don’t trigger the light because those photos or videos are not saved anywhere, including Gemini History. Before that media reaches the cloud, Google redacts faces from video feeds and filters out bystander voices. This processing is done by the companion app. Additionally, that media isn’t used to train AI models or target ads.

Other key specifications include four microphones and two open-ear speakers. Besides voice commands with the “Hey Gemini” hotword, there is a touchpad that accepts taps and swipes. A physical on/off switch lets you wear Intelligent Eyewear as regular glasses.

On iOS, Gemini can make calls, send 1:1 messages (including via iMessage), and receive notifications.

Battery life is rated at nine hours on a single charge, while there’s a charging case that stores seven charges. Features include turn-by-turn Google Maps directions and real-time translation. On the streaming front, there’s support for Apple Music, Spotify, YouTube Music, and Audible.

Google’s Android XR glasses require an iPhone 13 Pro or newer.

Warby Parker Intelligent Eyewear is available in three frame designs, starting at $395 for optical and sun styles. Gentle Monster Intelligent Eyewear is available in the US and South Korea from $449.

Pre-orders open today with retail availability on December 10.

#3172. Apple TV 4K (4th generation) review: Still waiting on Siri

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

Unlock and manage exclusive Tom’s Guide member rewards.

Join the Tom's Guide Club for quick access. Enter your email below and we'll send confirmation, and sign you up to our newsletter.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Apple TV 4K (4th gen) has a more powerful processor, support for full surround sound, and now has a lost remote finder. But it's the most expensive streaming device by far, and Siri still falls well short of Gemini and Alexa+ when it comes to finding what you want to watch.

Can create a 4-channel surround system with HomePod speakers

Siri not as good as Alexa+ or Gemini for surfacing content

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

The best streaming devices generally don’t get updated all that frequently; there’s not too much that changes year-to-year. It’s been four years since Apple released its last device, but now it’s back with the Apple TV 4K (4th gen).

This fourth-gen streamer has the company’s newest A19 processor — the same as in the iPhone 17 — which means it’s not only faster, but has access to the new-and-improved Siri, which in theory should mean that it’s easier for you to find shows to watch. And, you can also create a fully immersive surround-sound setup using HomePod smart speakers. But, the Apple TV 4K also comes with an exorbitantly high $299. Yes, it’s a nicer setup all around, but it’s hard to justify the price if you’re not in the Apple ecosystem.

At $299, the Apple TV 4K (4th generation) is by far the most expensive streaming device, and is a big jump in price over the 2022 model, whose most expensive variant cost $149 when it was first released (Apple jacked up the price to $249 earlier in 2026). Apple’s just offering one version this time, with 128GB of storage.

Among the best streaming devices, the next most expensive gadget is the Amazon Fire TV Cube, which costs $199 regularly.

Should you upgrade? Here are the major differences; for ease of comparison, I’m only including the 128GB version of the 2022 model.

Aside from the specs, the 2026 model supports up to four HomePod devices, whereas the 2022 model only supports two. In addition, the newer model has three mics, and its more powerful processor supports the newer, more advanced Siri.

The 4th-generation Apple TV 4K and its remote look identical to the previous model — a small black cube with ports on the back for HDMI, Ethernet, and power. One minor change is that the status LED is now in the middle, not that it’s all that noticeable.

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

Setup was a cinch; once I plugged in the Apple TV 4K, all I had to do was bring my iPhone near the device, and I was good to go within minutes. The Apple TV 4K even remembered all my installed apps from my previous Apple TV device. However, I did have to re-login to every app. If you have a lot of streaming services, this can get a bit tedious, no matter how easy they make it with QR codes.

One of the nicest upgrades is the new FindMy built into the remote; Apple’s remotes have long been easy to lose in the couch. You can use any iPhone to help locate the device and even have it play a little tone, but if you have an iPhone with Bluetooth 6 (the iPhone 17 or later), you can get super-precise location tracking.

I tried this with both an iPhone 14 Pro and an iPhone Air; with the 14 Pro, FindMy knew when I was close, but told me to look around. With the Air, the phone started buzzing more urgently the closer I got, and even gave me distance estimates. Finally, when I was within a few inches, it said “here.”

One thing that’s still missing from Apple’s remote though: backlit buttons.

Another benefit of the A19 chip in the Apple TV 4K (4th generation) is that it supports Apple Intelligence, which can be used for, among other things, finding what to watch. However, in my testing, it could use some work, especially when I compared it with Gemini on the Google TV Streamer and Alexa+ on the Fire TV Stick 4K.

My first stab with Siri was “Find me scary movies for kids.” I got a response saying “I’m not finding anything for that,” and offered to let me search YouTube.

I next tried “Find scary movies good for kids,” which did bring up some options, but I wouldn’t call “Poltergeist,” “Alien,” or “Seven” appropriate for my 8-year-old. I don't want her to know what's in the box just yet.

When I performed a similar search on the Google TV Streamer and on the Fire TV, I received much more relevant movies, such as “Coraline,” “Goosebumps 2,” “Hocus Pocus,” and “The Addams Family.”

I tried the same search another day on the Apple TV, and I got a few better suggestions, such as “Gremlins” and “Arachnophobia,” but the results still fell well short of what I hoped.

“What’s that movie with Audrey Hepburn that takes place in Rome” just returned a bunch of Christmas movies, none with Hepburn. On the Fire TV, Alexa+ brought up “Roman Holiday” in an instant, along with suggestions for other Hepburn movies.

Siri performed better when I asked it to “find action movies with Tom Hanks.” “Saving Private Ryan,” “Captain Philips,” “Angels & Demons,” and “Greyhound” were listed as the first few options.

Siri’s responses appear as a scrollable column along the right side of the screen, but there’s no audio reply. By comparison, on the Google TV Streamer, Gemini delivers the list, as well as a bit of dialogue, which makes everything feel friendlier overall.

Siri seemed to have a blind spot when it came to Netflix. I searched directly for “Top Gun: Maverick,” but Siri only showed that it was available through Paramount, when in fact you could also stream it on Netflix. Similarly, when I asked Siri for “The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo,” it only gave me options to buy or rent the movie, even though it was free to stream on Netflix.

A search for “KPop: Demon Hunters” was also fruitless. I either got a list of other movies with “demon hunters” in the title, or received this response: “I don’t have the answer for that, but I can search the web if you ask on your iPhone.” Siri was, however, able to find “The Queen’s Gambit” and “Love is Blind.”

Other things worked mostly as expected. “Turn off subtitles” worked within Apple TV, but not within the Netflix app. “Show my video Doorbell” brought up a live view from my doorbell’s camera. I could even place it in a small window in the corner while I watched other programs.

One of the best things in the Apple TV 4K’s favor is its far, far cleaner interface when compared with devices like the Fire TV, which are just littered with ads and sponsored content.

However, I wish it would go a little further than simply displaying a grid of apps; I do like how, on the Google TV Streamer and Fire TV, they both display a row of movies and shows currently airing, things I’ve recently been watching, and recommendations based on my viewing habits; it makes it easier to resume a binge session, and makes discovering new content a little easier.

The Apple TV 4K (4th generation) definitely felt a little snappier than the older model; while I didn’t time it, apps seemed to open faster.

Like the previous generation Apple TV 4K, the fourth-gen model lets you wirelessly connect Apple HomePods to use as an audio output. But, while the older model only let you connect two speakers, the fourth-gen Apple TV 4K lets you connect four, so you can have two front channels and two rear channels, for true surround sound.

The one caveat is that each pair has to match - that is, you need to have two HomePods or two Homepod minis as front channels. If you go the HomePod Mini route, you’ll spending around $600; I had two HomePod 2s as my front channels, and two HomePod Mini 2’s as my rears, which would mean an investment of just under $1,000. At that price, you may as well look at one of the best soundbars.

Amazon offers a similar feature with its streaming sticks, in that you can arrange a number of Echo Dots or Echo Studios to create a surround-sound system. I tried it with four Echo Studios, and it was pretty impressive.

The Apple TV 4K (4th generation) has some incremental upgrades over the previous model, but like I found with the HomeView, Siri as an AI assistant falls short of its rivals in Gemini and Alexa+.

In an era where there’s more movies and shows than ever to watch, an AI that’s capable of digging up something catered towards your tastes is essential. While I’m sure that Siri will improve over time, right now, you’re better off with a less expensive streaming stick, even if you do have to put up with some ads. The Roku Ultra, for example, costs half as much, yet offers support for Dolby Atmos and Dolby Vision.

One argument in the Apple TV 4K's favor is that it has 128GB of storage, which is far more than you get with other premium devices like the Google TV Streamer (32GB) and Fire TV Cube (16GB). But how many of us are still downloading movies?

The Apple TV 4K has some necessary upgrades, but until Siri gets better, it’s not a necessary upgrade.

#3170. Prediction: This Will Be SpaceX's Stock Price in 5 Years

It's growing fast, but the stock gains might be limited.

The S&P 500 has been volatile over the past few weeks, and it hasn't notched a new high in over a month. It's down 4% over the past month and up 9% year-to-date, ending its streak of annual double-digit gains for now.

The tech sector has been hit harder than others, and Space Exploration Technologies (SPCX +4.91%), or SpaceX, stock is down 11% from its first-day closing price. Let's check out where it could be in five years.

Despite its extraterrestrial name, SpaceX sees itself as more of an artificial intelligence (AI) company than anything else. Since Elon Musk merged SpaceX with xAI, the AI business is now part of the company, and the company's vast market opportunity belongs to this segment, which it has renamed Super Intelligence (SI).

The space business, though, is very exciting and is making rapid progress. The company is highly focused on perfecting fully reusable rockets, which would be a game changer for the space economy. Musk envisions sending the new Starship rocket into space weekly starting in 2027, and then twice weekly or more in the back half of the year. This is the only SpaceX segment that reported an operating loss in the third quarter, but reusable rockets will go a long way toward profitability.

It's also opening a new base in Louisiana with 20 launch towers and the ability to send millions of tons into space annually.

Looking five years out, SpaceX could be making several flights weekly using reusable technology and be fully profitable.

The Starlink satellite broadband business is the partner to the rocket business. It's the largest business of its kind, with 11,000 satellites in orbit, launched by SpaceX rockets and covering 190 countries. Musk believes that over the next three to five years, it will have 100 times the bandwidth it currently has. That equates to 100,000 satellites, or almost 10 times today's figure, each with 10 times more bandwidth.

It also plans to have a million Starlink mini data center satellites in the future.

Amazon is building a business to compete with Starlink, but it's much smaller. However, this is something to keep an eye on.

SI is the company's fastest-growing segment and where it sees its biggest opportunities. SI revenue increased 830% year over year in the third quarter, and it posted its first quarterly profit of $431 million.

SI includes the Grok AI model, the Cursor coding platform, and the Colossus data centers that drive AI development and generate rental revenue from clients like Anthropic and Alphabet.

SI has 1.7 GW (gigawatts) as of the third quarter, and Musk thinks it can reach 20 by the end of next year. In five years, it should be well beyond that. However, data center development might face some challenges as new lawmakers enter Congress and become governors in 2027. How regulations develop is unclear right now, and they might force an industry slowdown. SpaceX stock wasn't negatively affected by the news, since it already has a top position and plenty of power for the time being.

If SpaceX continues to grow fast and SI takes off, the company should be a lot bigger in five years. There are two reasons I'm hesitant to recommend it as an investment.

The first is the unknown. It sure looks as if AI is going to keep growing fast, but there could be many new developments that hinder SpaceX's expected growth, such as new technology and cheaper competition.

It's also extremely expensive, trading at a price-to-sales ratio of 58, and that ratio keeps falling as revenue rises and the stock price goes down. It will likely continue to decline, which limits how high the price can go.

However, the stock's value could still be much higher in five years. SpaceX revenue increased 161% year over year in the third quarter, and Wall Street is looking for 270% next year. If the company can grow at a compound annual growth rate of much less than that, say 50%, over the next five years, it would have $247 billion in trailing 12-month sales. At a price-to-sales ratio of 20, it would have a $4.9 trillion market cap, or 150% more than today's figure, and the stock would be worth $357.

#3169. Alpine Linux and OpenSSH patch flaw that’s as bad as it can get

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

This dangerous Linux security hole must be patched as soon as possible.

The perfect nightmare scenario for a Linux server is when all an attacker needs to do is reach the server’s Secure Shell (SSH) port, waltz right in, and take it over. That’s what happened to Alpine Linux, the popular, lightweight Linux server. Adding insult to injury, this happened only days after Alpine Linux dodged a security hole-sized bullet to its GitLab implementation.

Also: Linux Mint 27 arrives next month, and I like it already: What to expect

How bad is it? As bad as it can get. Alpine Linux explained in its security advisory that if an attacker can reach a vulnerable server’s SSH port, they can get in “with one connection,” and the attack “works every time, and needs no retries.”

As security engineer Gregory Bryant explained in his LinkedIn post:

Most authentication bypasses come from complex logic chains, but yesterday’s Alpine Linux OpenSSH vulnerability (CVE-2026-123158) comes down to a single character: *.”

If you run Alpine Linux (or another musl-based distro) with the default openssh-server package (no Pluggable Authentication Modules (PAM)) and PasswordAuthentication enabled, an attacker can log into password-disabled, or key-only accounts simply by sending a password between 257 and 1024 bytes long.

Alpine Linux isn’t the only operating system that uses musl, a lightweight version of the standard C library (libc). Other operating systems that use musl and are potentially vulnerable include Adélie Linux; Void Linux; Sabotage Linux; OpenWrt, an Android variant,  and the Yocto Project, which is used to build embedded Linux distributions.

Also: This clever banking scam keeps phishing by faking its own demise

Wind River, which produces the commercial embedded Linux distro, Wind River Linux, is also looking into the issue. A company representative told me, “Wind River takes security seriously. We are actively reviewing the reported vulnerability and assessing its potential impact. We will take appropriate action as needed.”

Behind the scenes, when OpenSSH is built without PAM, it verifies passwords by hashing the password attempt using the C library’s crypt() function. It then compares the result to the account’s stored password field. So far, so good.

But when a key is longer than 256 bytes, musl’s crypt() function returns the string * as an error indicator. That is also what the password field holds for any account with no password, such as a key-only account. Thus, the “hash” matches and the login succeeds, and the attacker walks in.

Also: The new Cutefish Linux distro might be the best MacOS clone around

To exploit it, an attacker only needs the name of such an account. The attacker also needs at least one other account on the machine with a 5 or 6 password hash, and then to send a password of 257 to 1,024 bytes. According to Alpine, one user with a password is enough to make every passwordless account accessible.

In Linux systems that use glibc’s crypt(), which is almost all of them, the same attempt would return NULL on error, which sshd already rejects, so Debian, Ubuntu, Fedora, etc., aren’t affected.

According to *sshole, the group that uncovered the problem, this is a side effect that has been hiding since 2016.

Alpine said every release it checked is affected: 3.21 through 3.24, edge, and the older 3.16 to 3.20 branches. Exposure requires the following:

Root is not directly exposed in most cases. It has shipped as root:* in the base image since about Alpine 3.16, but OpenSSH’s default PermitRootLogin prohibit-password blocks it. Another account that can become root, for example through doas, still gives an attacker a route to root.

Alpine singled out its official tiny-cloud images, versions 3.18.11 through 3.24.3, as especially vulnerable. These ship with an alpine user with a * password field and passwordless doas. They are safe on first boot but become exploitable once any 6 hash exists on the machine. That can happen when an administrator sets a console password or when user data adds a user with a hashed password, which means, essentially, all of them.

Alpine released 3.21.10, 3.22.8, 3.23.8 and 3.24.4 on Thursday, with the OpenSSH fix among the security changes. It also published fixed packages for each release back to 3.16. Alpine 3.21 reached end of support on Nov. 1.

The just-released OpenSSH 10.6p2 avoids the problem in sshd. Alpine’s stable branches carry a patch for the same problem. You should run apk upgrade -U -a and then restart the daemon with rc-service sshd restart. Alpine stressed that upgrading the package does not replace the running daemon. Anyone who cannot update should set PasswordAuthentication no and restart sshd, after confirming that key login works.

Also: Maze Linux is the best security-focused distro I’ve ever tested

To check for an attack, Alpine told administrators to search /var/log/messages for “Accepted password for” lines that name an account with no password. It also advised reviewing dedicated OpenBSD application subexecutor (doas) use and recently created users, files, and authorized keys. “If you cannot rule out a login, treat the machine as compromised.” Just what you wanted for your weekend, I know, but here we are.

#3167. The Best Uranium Stocks to Buy and Hold as Nuclear Power Expands

Over 30 nations have pledged to triple their nuclear energy capacity, which should serve as a long-term tailwind for these uranium stocks.

Countries worldwide have committed to massively expanding their nuclear energy capabilities. At COP30, over 33 nations committed to tripling global nuclear energy capacity by 2050. With strong long-term tailwinds, uranium stocks like Cameco (CCJ -3.15%) and Uranium Energy (UEC -3.11%) are well positioned for the long haul.

This massive expansion of nuclear energy comes as countries grapple with growing energy needs and decarbonization goals. While renewables have expanded significantly, many forms of it only provide intermittent power, not the 24/7, reliable baseload power that data centers, warehouses, and manufacturing facilities require.

Here's why these two uranium stocks could be smart buy-and-hold options today.

Cameco is one of the world's largest providers of uranium fuel and owns high-grade assets, including the Cigar Lake and McArthur River mines, the Key Lake mill, and the Blind River refinery. Cameco is appealing to investors because of its massive scale, long-term contracts, and investment across the nuclear value chain.

Cameco generally doesn't sell uranium in spot markets. Instead, the company maintains contracts to sell an average of 28 million pounds of uranium annually through 2030, with more volume contracted in the next couple of years. Management is intentionally keeping volumes uncommitted in the longer term to capture the potential upside from rising prices.

The company's operations span mining, milling, and processing (separating uranium minerals from rock to create yellowcake), refining yellowcake to remove impurities, and converting the powder into the compounds used in nuclear reactors. The company also holds a 49% stake in Global Laser Enrichment, which develops laser-based uranium enrichment technology.

In addition, Cameco owns 49% of Westinghouse Electric, one of the world's largest nuclear hardware suppliers. Westinghouse also manufactures the AP1000 reactors used in traditional power plants and should be a major beneficiary of the nuclear energy build-out in the coming decades.

While Cameco takes a more measured approach to spot uranium prices and the nuclear value chain, Uranium Energy is a U.S.-based uranium miner that offers greater upside if uranium prices rise. That's because the company is completely unhedged. During its 2026 fiscal year (ending July 31), Uranium Energy realized what it claims is an industry-leading $93 per pound on the 400,000 pounds it sold.

Uranium Energy is pursuing a low-cost, hub-and-spoke in-situ recovery (ISR) model to restart U.S. uranium production. The hub is its centralized processing facility, where it turns uranium concentrate into yellowcake. Meanwhile, the spokes surround satellite deposits, where the company pumps a solution underground to dissolve uranium in place and then pumps the uranium-rich solution to the surface.

By leveraging ISR and hub-and-spoke infrastructure, Uranium Energy can bring new spokes online without building new mills, drying facilities, or other costly investments for uranium refining. Additionally, the company is taking steps to become a fully integrated nuclear fuel producer, like Cameco, by resolving a massive bottleneck in uranium conversion. It hopes to begin producing commercially here by the 2030s.

For aggressive investors seeking unhedged upside to spot uranium prices, Uranium Energy is a top pick. But be warned: This effect works both ways, and if uranium prices decline meaningfully, earnings would fall right alongside them.

#3166. Samsung’s new SmartTag 3 debuts with next-gen Bluetooth – and one big problem

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

The Galaxy SmartTag 3 supports emerging Bluetooth tracking tech, but it's not a match for Samsung's OS exclusivity.

Samsung’s Galaxy SmartTag 3 is now available for purchase in the US, promising a smaller, lighter design than previous generations, compatibility with iOS devices, 550 days of battery life, an NFC-powered Lost Mode, Left Behind Alerts, and an IP67 dust- and water-resistant rating.

Though the Galaxy SmartTag 3 is compatible with iOS devices, the features available to Apple fans are limited, with Ring Phone, Left Behind Alerts, and Compass View reserved for Galaxy users. Compass View is enabled by Bluetooth Channel Sounding, an upgraded Bluetooth distance-finding technology. Despite Samsung embracing a low-cost boost to device tracking, Channel Sounding is locked inside the Galaxy ecosystem, a blow to the technology’s intended purpose.

Also: 3 ways Bluetooth 7 upgrades your devices beyond lossless audio

Channel Sounding is also Google’s Pixel Tag and Motorola’s Moto Tag 2, but these manufacturers open the technology to all compatible Android phones. However, Samsung’s SmartTag 3 doesn’t rely on Android’s vast but fragmented Find My Device network; instead, Samsung’s take on Channel Sounding will rely exclusively on the Galaxy Find Network. If a semi-closed ecosystem can help make evolving Bluetooth tech more reliable, does it matter that its implementation is counterproductive?

Samsung is the Goldilocks of device ecosystems. It’s not considered a walled garden like Apple, but it’s not as open to full third-party interoperability as Google. Many of Samsung’s most useful features are reserved for use within its Galaxy ecosystem. However, Samsung’s OS is built on top of Android, allowing for more flexibility than iOS, but still offering OS-exclusive features and, more importantly, feature reliability.

Full access to Samsung’s Galaxy Find Network is exclusive to Galaxy devices, similar to how full access to Apple’s Find My tracking features is reserved for Apple devices. On the other hand, Google’s Find Hub can accommodate Android phones from several manufacturers, including Samsung.

Also: Android is getting my favorite iOS tracking feature – what to expect

According to a press release, nearly 900 million Galaxy devices exist on the Galaxy Find Network. Each one’s constant Bluetooth signals contribute to an expansive network of crowdsourced data, extending the Galaxy FindTag 3’s reach and surfacing location data faster.

Google’s Find Hub’s greatest benefit is its scale: it can work with headphones, earbuds, Bluetooth trackers, smartphones, and smartwatches from multiple manufacturers.

However, different ecosystems limit tracking features to basic functionality, showing only where a device was last seen before it was powered off, or emitting a chime if you lose it. Live location data and accurate direction and distance finding from your smartphone aren’t possible.

Also: Apple has a Bluetooth problem, and Android is taking advantage

Implementing Bluetooth Channel Sounding aims to break down ecosystem-specific barriers, especially in a device-tracking context. If your smartphone, headphones, and smartwatch all support Channel Sounding, you could access fine-ranging tracking on all of them, regardless of device manufacturer.

Despite Samsung’s ecosystem providing it a device-tracking advantage, it defeats the purpose of Bluetooth: democratization. Basic Bluetooth connectivity allows any Bluetooth-compatible device to connect to another; that’s why you can wirelessly pair a pair of AirPods with a Lenovo laptop.

Also: Google’s Pixel Tag tracker has a big advantage over AirTags

Channel Sounding’s goal is no different in that it aims to bring more accurate distance awareness to Bluetooth-enabled devices, allowing you to finely track a pair of Sony headphones with an iPhone — that’s the goal, but not yet reality.

Samsung instead adopted Channel Sounding for its first consumer-ready endpoint within the boundaries of its ecosystem. Only Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra, Galaxy Z Fold 8, Galaxy S26 Ultra, and Galaxy S26 Plus users can unlock the Galaxy SmartTag 3’s Channel Sounding capabilities when engaging its Compass View feature.

Also: Beware of Bluetooth sniffers: How your favorite gadgets could be exposing your data

All of these phones support Bluetooth 6.0 and Channel Sounding, but the Galaxy SmartTag 3’s Channel Sounding abilities will only be available to them and future Galaxy phones with Channel Sounding.

Conversely, Google’s Pixel Tag offers Channel Sounding to all Android phones that support it, including Galaxy phones. The result is that the Galaxy SmartTag 3 will operate just like any other Bluetooth tracker when paired with a base-model flagship phone, an older Galaxy phone, or an iPhone.

During this year’s WWDC, Apple announced Channel Sounding support for iPhones with its N1 networking chip and third-party Bluetooth 6.3 devices. Bluetooth 6.3 devices aren’t on the market yet and won’t be for a few years.

I assume Apple’s announcement of faraway future support is to give itself time to decide how Channel Sounding will fit into its walled garden, similar to Samsung’s implementation in the Galaxy SmartTag 3.

Also: How to tell if a hidden AirTag is tracking you – and disable it ASAP

Sure, Google’s Find Hub still needs some maturing; just last year, Google boosted the opt-in opportunities to add more devices for crowdsourced data, Find People is coming to Wear OS, and Find Hub is getting “Notify when left behind” alerts soon.

Apple’s and Samsung’s device location networks may be more feature-rich thanks to their closed ecosystems, but Google is working toward a truly open, easy-to-use network of devices powered by Channel Sounding. Which one is more important to you is for you to decide when it’s time to make a purchase.

#3165. Half of New Games on Steam Are Now Made With AI. How Does This Reflect the Gaming Industry?

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Most of those games are unpopular, with 10 or fewer reviews from gamers.

Steam, the digital marketplace for PC games from game studio Valve, has hit a major milestone, sparking pushback from parts of the gaming community: Approximately 50% of new Steam games in October were made with the help of AI.

This underscores a growing trend in gaming, where more games are made with some form of AI assistance — specifically, generative AI, which developers have used to generate code, art assets, voice lines and more. Developers are adopting the technology in increasing numbers.

The numbers come from a Reddit user who goes by Ploz, and who used Steam’s publicly available data to see how many newly released games relied on AI in some capacity. This was possible because of Valve’s AI disclosure policy for newly released games, which requires developers to state whether they used AI in making their game. The disclosure is part of the storefront’s publicly accessible records, allowing anyone to view it.

A Valve representative did not respond to a request for comment.

The data is a snapshot of the tidal wave of AI-made games flooding storefronts, most prominently Steam. But crucially, Valve has chosen not to limit this flood, washing its hands of the problem and leaving gamers to fend for themselves in finding quality games. Developers had already been struggling to get their games noticed, and Valve’s limited curation seems completely unprepared for the firehose of AI-made games churned out on an increasing scale.

Valve implemented the AI disclosure policy in January 2024 to increase developer transparency. At the time, only 1.4% of newly released games used AI. This increased to 13.4% by the end of 2024, then to 24% by the end of 2025. It now sits at 49.9%.

There are some caveats. The AI disclosure is only required for games that use AI to create player-facing content, such as artwork, sound, character dialogue and localization. The 49.9% figure is specific to these types of games and doesn’t account for developers who use AI for behind-the-scenes tasks such as coding and bug fixes. A Google Cloud survey conducted in August 2025 showed that 87% of developers use AI for backend work, which doesn’t require disclosure on Steam.

So it’s likely that the number of games on Steam built with AI assistance is greater than 50%. Ploz notes that the only way users can avoid AI-generated games is to manually check for AI disclosures.

According to Ploz, the most common use of AI in game development is for artwork, which was mentioned in 63% of disclosures. Text and translations gobbled up 30%, while music (21%), code (16%) and voices (7%) rounded out the list. Many developers had more than one of those areas named in their disclosure, and about a quarter of developers said they were using AI for their Steam store pages and marketing.

About 3% of developers used AI directly as a game mechanic. One such example is a driving simulator called Teach My Little Sister How to Drive. Developers use AI in the game to interpret a player’s voice commands and generate the sister’s responses. To keep a playable demo of the game available to the public, the development team, Easy Fox, is paying $1,000 every day just to cover these AI operating costs — an expense so high that it was forced to take out a loan simply to keep the demo running.

For development, there are loads of options. The Unity 6 engine came out in October 2024 and includes AI code assistance, AI asset generation and third-party integration with Claude Code, Gemini and Grok. Anthropic’s Claude is a fairly popular option among smaller developers, since it supports the ability to vibe code whole games, with ChatGPT, Gemini and GitHub Copilot as other options.

Many of the games being released with the AI disclosure on Steam can be classified as slop — a derogatory term gamers have applied liberally to titles that heavily lean on generative AI for development and look derivative of other popular games. According to Ploz, most AI-enabled games are small: Around 47% of new games with fewer than 10 reviews have an AI disclosure. Among developers who released more than 10 games in a year, 68% of those games included the disclosure.

Games with AI disclosures received fewer positive reviews on average than those without. And among all newly released games with more than 1,000 reviews, only 17% include an AI disclosure. That means gamers are still gravitating toward games without an AI disclosure and pushing back against games that use the technology.

Developers seem aware of this. CNET reached out to two dozen well-known developers, including Epic Games, EA, Activision Blizzard, Ubisoft, PlayStation Studios and many others. All of them declined to comment.

Bigger studios may be using AI in their development, but it’s hard to tell the scale. There’s no such thing as an AI audit yet, and the industry seems to be relying on voluntary disclosure for now. Steam’s disclosure policy has outed smaller developers who are either worried about violating the policy and being taken off the digital storefront, or aren’t worried about the negative effects of disclosure.

A lot of dominoes had to fall for this to happen. The availability of AI tools and the increasing ease of use are definite contributors. Subreddits like r/AIGameDev have plenty of examples of people putting together games with just a few days or weeks of vibe coding, which is a lot shorter than the standard video game development cycle, which can stretch over years depending on the scale, production level and graphics quality. This practice has exploded over the last couple of years, resulting in a lot of games getting launched that are made mostly or entirely with AI.

Many of these games end up on Steam, which doesn’t have a policy limiting AI-developed games.

“Digital storefronts like Steam have already struggled to moderate low-effort and poor-quality games, as well as copycats stealing other games’ ideas,” said CNET Managing Editor David Lumb.

Valve openly admits its role in this, stating that the problem definitely exists but that the company doesn’t “want to be gatekeepers telling developers which tools they should or shouldn’t use.”

It takes a similar stance on AI cloning, with Valve’s Tom Giardino telling developers that “you must continue to grow your game by adding features, personality and creativity that stem from your own perspective as a developer.”

These policies essentially allow any AI-developed game or clone to reach the Valve storefront without pushback, which certainly contributes to the flood of newly released games with some form of player-facing AI involvement in their development.

Rival store Epic Games has a similar stance, allowing basically any game that wants to be there. The company declined to comment further about this, but CEO Tom Sweeney is an avid supporter of AI in video game development, stating that it was “perfectly logical” for developers to rely on AI to handle the mundane grunt work that takes up most of a developer’s time.

While Steam and Epic Games tend to take a more lax attitude toward AI slop, other storefronts like Itch.io are not. Itch.io has a whole policy against AI slop and the company has willingly, and at times gleefully, deleted terabytes of AI slop from its storefront. It also requires developers to disclose if they used AI but takes a much more consumer-friendly approach by letting users filter those out of search results if they don’t want to see them.

Some measures are being taken to address the proliferation of AI slop, but none will entirely stop the problem. Cloning has been a problem for many years. Mobile gamers of a certain vintage may remember the flock of Flappy Bird clones that appeared on app stores after the original game went down, and those weren’t even made with AI.

AI makes cloning much easier and faster, and some AI companies are addressing it. Anthropic recently changed Claude Opus 5.5 to prevent it from generating copies of existing games. Anthropic engineering leader Addy Osmani posted on X that using Claude to copy games infringes on intellectual property rights and violates Anthropic’s policy.

However, during CNET’s testing, we found we could still make games resembling popular titles, so cloning remains possible with a little creativity.

“This has come up over and over on the subreddit r/GameDev, and there’s no real solution if Steam and other digital storefronts don’t stem the flood of low-quality AI games drowning out the labors of love that entertain and innovate,” Lumb said.

Many developers openly oppose AI and refuse to use it in their own work. However, as the Steam stats show, that crowd’s output appears to be getting smaller and smaller every year amid the unending stream of AI games.

#3163. We’ve Folded the iPhone Duo Almost 400,000 Times. How Much More Can It Take?

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Our Fold-a-Phone machine folds Apple's iPhone Duo 900 times every hour to test the durability of its hinge.

We’re now a third of the way through November, and the machine in CNET’s lab continues to work overtime testing Apple’s first folding phone, the $1,999 iPhone Duo. We purchased this poor phone more than two weeks ago, and since then its only job has been to bend and flatten, bend and flatten, until it breaks.

So how many times can we fold the iPhone Duo? As of 3 p.m. on Tuesday, Nov. 10, we’re at 390,000 folds, and by tomorrow we’ll reach 400,000 folds.

I oversee hardware and software testing as director of lab operations in our lab in Louisville, Kentucky. Over the last week, I’ve seen a lot of chatter about the sturdiness of the Duo’s folding hinge and its potential to fail or crack. I’ve periodically examined the Duo we’re testing in our machine, and so far, I haven’t seen any signs of damage. And the crease isn’t any more visible than it was when we took it out of the box. If that changes, I’ll let you know here and on our livestream.

In the meantime, let me explain what we’re doing. My team and I designed and built a proprietary machine to test foldable phones like Apple’s and its Samsung rival, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 (which we’ve also started testing). I’ve worked on the methodology and build of this testing rig for months in anticipation of Apple’s long-rumored foldable iPhone.

We even named our machine to match its purpose: Meet the Fold-a-Phone.

Now, my team of engineers and testing experts will watch the iPhone Duo open and close, open and close, to rigorously and systematically monitor the durability of Apple’s hinge and two screens.

After all, repeatedly folding a phone with bare hands can only get you so far in understanding the complex forces at play between the magnetics that snap the screen shut and the all-critical hinge.

CNET’s Senior Technology Reporter, Abrar Al-Heeti, has done a beautiful job capturing the iPhone Duo’s pros and cons in her smart, thorough review. Our Fold-a-Phone machine will add a deep data foundation to complement her real-world experience.

Since Apple hasn’t publicly shared claims of the iPhone Duo’s foldable lifespan, CNET’s Fold-a-Phone machine is poised to provide a wealth of valuable data about Apple’s first foldable phone and competing models in the foldable market.

And yes, you’d better believe we will use our treasure trove of in-house data to share status updates and comparisons during our ongoing testing window with the Duo.

Join CNET’s iPhone Duo livestream on YouTube weekdays from 1 p.m. to 5 p.m. ET, where you can follow along live and watch the Fold-a-Phone do its thing to a Duo.

The importance of this moment is hard to overstate. Apple’s appearance on the foldable smartfold frontier lags Samsung by seven years (the first Galaxy Fold went on sale in the US in September 2019). Motorola and other phone-makers have long experimented with foldable phones in every shape and size, including a trifold accordion foldable phone we first demoed in 2019.

CNET’s mobile experts, including Al-Heeti and Editor at Large Andrew Lanxon, have discussed the legitimizing effect of the iPhone Duo’s existence on the entire foldable phone landscape, which has previously felt like a new-wave fantasy rather than a mainstream riptide.

In many ways, Apple’s newfound competition with existing foldable phones completes the portfolio. That is precisely why we’re building the Fold-a-Phone now, and why our proprietary machine, methodology and test data will enrich our collective understanding of the capabilities – and yes, limitations – of foldable phones as our true next-generation mobile device.

Most current foldable phones are rated for 200,000 to 500,000 folds. As such, we knew we needed to create a robust and adaptable machine that could accommodate book- and flip-style foldable phones of any size, dimension and hinge orientation. (Note: The Fold-a-Phone was not built for trifold phones, which present a unique element to the engineering challenge.)

Moreover, we wanted to test the phone the way people would actually use it. No one just sits around opening and closing their foldable phone at top speed all day. Rather, you open it naturally, spend a few minutes watching a video, browsing a web page, or using an app, close it, and then put it in your pocket. This may happen dozens of times per day.

Mimicking this usage on the Fold-a-Phone limits undue stress on the phone hinge and avoids generating excess heat compared to a test built for speed.

We determined that a cadence of roughly 4 seconds could sidestep technical hurdles while also being reasonably fast. The foldable phone takes 1 second to open, 1 second to fully open, 1 second to close and 1 second to fully close. This cycle counts as a single completed fold. Then, the cycle repeats until either the hinge or the screen gives out.

In conceptualizing and building the Fold-a-Phone, our team has used standard, off-the-shelf components to simplify the machine’s development. The essential design consists of two armatures, distinctly designed to perform the opening and closing movements with both force and grace.

An industrial-grade stepper motor drives each armature, with the host software (running on a connected computer) deterministically adjusting the torque to complete each step of the process while also protecting the phone. If any of the several proximity sensors fail to detect the armature in the correct position, the machine stops immediately.

We also monitor the motors’ power usage to track how well the foldable phone opens and closes over time. We have set up cameras to capture images and video of the test from multiple angles, and we will analyze regular status updates from the computer to determine the current status of the phone and the test.

To ensure we never miss a major development, the entire rig is connected to an EcoFlow Delta 3 Plus power station to guard against electricity outages, and all the output data is saved to multiple locations.

To secure each phone to the machine, we use our CNET Lab Test-winning 3D printer, the Prusa Core One, to 3D-print a custom “sled” that matches each phone’s exact dimensions. We secure the phone to the sled with heavy-duty double-sided tape (yes, it works!) and then screw the sled onto the machine.

There’s always room for improvement. We’re constantly looking for ways to make the machine run more smoothly and quietly without disrupting the folding rhythm.

Apple’s presence is already changing the game and could very well spur innovation in ways we can’t predict today. But until then, our Fold-a-Phone machine will continue to test the iPhone Duo and its competitors, and CNET’s writers will report on how well these individual hinged devices stand up to the challenge – or fold under pressure.

#3162. Android Auto requires Android 11 or higher now – check your compatibility

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Tech > Services & Software > Operating Systems > Mobile OS > Android

Android Auto's minimum requirements have changed. Here's what to know.

Google has officially phased out support for Android 9 and Android 10 for wired Android Auto use — so you’ll need Android 11 at a minimum to connect an Android phone to a compatible car via USB, according to an update to Google’s Android Auto support page spotted by Android Authority. Android 11 through Android 17, the most up-to-date version, are fully supported for Android Auto (though Android 17’s adoption rate remains quite low).

These changes confirm early reports that Android 10 users saw warnings that their devices would soon lose Android Auto support, even before Google’s documentation had specified the change.

Also: Got an old car? Android Auto is easy to add: 2 ways, starting at $20

It’s not uncommon for Google to drop the oldest Android versions that can still run Android Auto every few years. In 2024, Android 8, released in 2017, was dumped from service. Android 11 was first released in 2020.

Android Auto brings apps to your car display so that drivers can focus better on the road. It allows you to control features such as navigation, maps, calls, text messages, and music, and is the Android equivalent of Apple CarPlay.

Also: 5 Android Auto apps that make my life easier on the road

The requirements have changed little since last year, aside from the new minimum software requirement. The new instructions for wired Android Auto support are straightforward: Phones must be running Android 11 (Red Velvet Cake) or newer, have an active data plan, and be supported by a compatible car. Google also recommends a quality USB cable.

Android Auto is integrated into compatible phones, so you do not need to download it. Android Auto isn’t available on devices that run Android (Go edition).

Also: I was a big wireless Android Auto fan, until I tried wired – now I won’t go back

To find out if your car or stereo is compatible with Android Auto, Google has a hub page to help. For more information about your car’s compatibility with Android Auto on your car display, it’s best to contact your vehicle manufacturer.

For drivers still using older phones running Android 9 or Android 10, getting Android Auto back will require either replacing a current device with one that runs Android 11 or newer, or installing an available software update on a current device.
